en: The Fourth Uddyota.

Thus, having explained *dhvani* in detail for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions, the Fourth Uddyota of the *Locana* [concludes] that very explanation; for even while engaged in the fulfillment of the fivefold duties, the Supreme Lord [remains].
I bow to that power of Śaṅkara which does not depend on any other external instrument.
In order to establish the connection with the subsequent section, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) says: "Thus," and "another purpose.
Although the purpose has already been stated by the phrase "for the delight of the hearts of sensitive readers" (*sahṛdayamanaḥprītaye*), [he states it again].
And although it was already somewhat clarified in the third chapter that one may either compose or understand good poetry,
nevertheless, an effort is now made to make it even more explicit,
so that it may be understood with perfect clarity.
Therefore, it is said that there is another purpose: that the clear delineation [of poetry] appears entirely different from this indistinctly delineated [preliminary stage].
Alternatively, the "difference" (antara) between the two previously mentioned purposes—that is, their distinction—is being stated:
by what distinction does the composition of excellent poetry constitute its purpose?

And by what means is the specific understanding of good poetry (*satkāvyabodha*) defined? Thus is the distinction determined. Now begins the commentary on the fourth chapter (*udyota*), the "Light on Meaning" (*arthodyota*), of the *Locana* according to my own judgment; I shall explain it somewhat, may the wise be gracious toward me herein. *Bālapriyā*: Now the commentary on the fourth chapter (*udyota*) begins. Regarding the "Light on Meaning" (*arthodyota*) in the fourth [chapter] of the *Locana*, I shall provide some explanation according to my intellect; may the learned be pleased with me in this matter.
Regarding the word *kṛtya*:
it refers to the fivefold function consisting of emanation (*sṛṣṭi*) and so forth.
As it has been said: "The fivefold function of that [Lord] who is eternally risen is declared to be emanation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and likewise the act of bestowing grace."
The connection is that [He acts] "without depending on any other instrument" by means of that illusory form (*māyārūpa*).
The meaning is that He accomplishes creation and so forth while depending solely upon that very illusory form.
Regarding the phrase "the connection with the internal illumination":
this means the connection of the fourth chapter with the third chapter.

Anticipating the objection that it is improper to speak of a "different purpose" since the very purpose previously stated is what is about to be explained, he provides the resolution beginning with "Even though," and so forth.

Now, one might object: "Even though a purpose consisting of pleasure has already been stated, what is about to be described must be something different from that. To this he says: "The third," and so forth. "That very thing" means "the purpose itself."
"In order to make it more manifest"— the word "that very same" is to be supplied here. "Is understood."
The word "to be described" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "From this," and so forth.
[This refers to] that which has been indistinctly determined.
The word "purpose" (prayojanāt) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].

By the statement that "dhvani must be discerned with effort by virtuous persons who are properly engaged in either composing or understanding good poetry," it is obtained by implication that the discernment of dhvani is the purpose for both the composition and the knowledge of good poetry; therefore, the meaning is that this purpose has not been explicitly stated.
"Clear exposition" means it has been stated clearly.
He explains it by another method, beginning with "Alternatively," and so forth.
This is an elaboration of what was just stated— beginning with "by what specific distinction," and so forth.
The word "asya" (of this) means "of the exposition of *dhvani*."
Another purpose is stated:

"The path of Suggestive Poetry (dhvani) that has been shown, along with its subordinated suggestives (saguṇībhūtavyaṅgya), brings about infinity for the quality of the poets' creative intuition (pratibhā). (DhvK 4.1)

The path of suggestion (dhvani), along with that of the subordinated suggestible (saguṇībhūtavyaṅgya), which has been demonstrated, causes the quality of the poets' creative intuition (pratibhā) to attain infinity. // 1 //
This path of sound and its subordinate suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) which has been elucidated has another fruit: the infinity of the poet’s creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
If one asks how this is so—it is because [speech] adorned by even one of these modes [is thus infinite].
Speech attains a state of novelty, even when it possesses a connection with previously expressed meanings.
Therefore, even if it possesses the connection of a prior meaning, speech attains freshness when adorned by even one of these modes. (2)

Regarding the question of how this [work] functions in the composition of excellent poetry (*satkāvyakaraṇa*), it must first be stated that what has already been accomplished is what is to be known; therefore, it is said:
"That which belongs to *dhvani*... (1).
One might object, with the intention that this [statement] is misplaced because there is an infinite variety of intuitions due to the differences among sounds (*dhvani*), by asking: "How so?
To this, the reply is: "For this reason" (*ato hi*).
Let alone the fact that there are many varieties.
The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that it occurs even by means of a single [word].
This is what is being said: inspired eloquence (*pratibhāna*) is a particular kind of wisdom (*prajñā*) grounded in the object to be described.

Since that which is to be described is limited and has already been touched upon by the first poet alone, the inspired eloquence regarding it for everyone else would necessarily be of the same nature as his.

Consequently, since poetry (*kāvyam*) is also of that same nature, the usage of poets has now become corrupted; however, by means of the aforementioned variety of expression, those very meanings become limitless, and thus the infinity of the creative intuitions (*pratibhā*) directed toward them is logically established. Now, one might ask: what is the fruit of this infinity of intuition? To determine this, it was stated that "the speech attains novelty."

By that, the novelty of poetic utterances— that is, of poetic sentences— is attained; and that [novelty] arises when there is an infinity of creative intuition (pratibhā), which in turn arises when there is an infinity of meanings (artha).
"And that [is] due to the varieties of *dhvani*. Regarding "How is this its function?":
the meaning is, "In what way is the exposition of *dhvani* useful?"
The connection is with the words "this is that. // 1 // // //
"Having different loci" (vyadhikaraṇa) means "incoherent.
He indicates the word "even" (api) in the phrase "by even one [of them]" with the words "let alone" (āsatām).
This is what is meant:
by the second half of the first verse and by the second verse, the essential meaning (bhāvārtha) that is about to be stated is demonstrated; this is the sense.
He states that very point with the words "to be described," and so forth.

Up to the words "due to the differentiation of resonance" [it is explained that] it is a particular kind of wisdom (prajñāviśeṣa) directed toward the object to be described— that is, having as its object this or that specific thing which is to be described.
The meaning is "having the form of a manifestation. The word "of the poet" is to be supplied. "Of that same kind" means:
The meaning is: "of the same nature as the creative intuition (*pratibhāna*) of the first poet.
"Of that very nature" means:
"of the very same nature as the poetry of the first poet."
The word "iti" indicates the reason; "bhraṣṭa" (fallen) is to be connected with the verb "syāt" (would be).
"By the aforementioned variety" means by the variety of *dhvani* (suggestion) and *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion). "Of the utterances" is explained as "of poetic sentences."
The word *iti* marks the conclusion.

Therefore, when speech is adorned by even one of the aforementioned varieties of *dhvani*, it attains a sense of novelty (*navatvam*), even though it touches upon a subject already composed by ancient poets.

For instance, in the case of *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), there is a sense of novelty through the employment of its two types, even while following a prior theme.

For instance: "A slightly charming smile, the power of a glance tremulous and sweet, the movement of speech fresh with the essence of playful dalliance, the onset of gait fragrant with budding grace—what indeed is not beautiful in the fawn-eyed maiden as she touches upon her youth?"
Regarding that, the *Locana* first states the instance of "entirely concealed denotation" (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*) in the verse beginning with "smile" (*smitam*).
Here, the touch of the fragrance that has blossomed with the essence of charming sweetness is entirely concealed.

By means of these [qualities], there are manifested: beauty not derived from elsewhere, being beloved by all people, inexhaustible expansion, the quelling of distress and the providing of satisfaction, tenderness, universality, the persistence of those refinements, and the state of being desirable through effort.

It should be understood that in all such cases, whatever is accomplished by those suggested meanings— such as a smile and so forth— in the form of a different quality (dharma) than the well-known quality prescribed for elders,
that very thing becomes an unprecedented (apūrva) merit. This is to be maintained everywhere.

The connection with the distant [conclusion] is: "Thus, it is precisely its unprecedented nature that shines forth. Regarding the word *asmitam* in *bālapriyā*: *kiñcit smitam* means a slight smile, or a gentle smile.
The phrase "it becomes charming" (*mugdhaṃ bhavati*) is to be supplied everywhere as the remainder [of the sentence].
"Taralamadhura" means both tremulous and sweet.
"Dṛṣṭivibhava" means a vision distinguished by its splendor.
*Parispandaḥ* means expansion.
It is full of sap through the waves—the successions of ever-arising, momentary particularities—which are those novel charms (*vilāsas*).

It is such that the fragrance of play (*līlā-parimala*) belonging to the sprouts (*kisalaya*) has blossomed there. This is according to the etymological derivation from the root *muh*, meaning "to delude."
The primary meaning of the word *mugdha* is either "causing delusion," as characterized by the phrase "deluded by youth and passion," or "innocence";
likewise, the primary meanings of words such as *madhura* (sweet), *vibhāva* (determinant emotion), and so forth, are "the essence of the sweet rasa" and "sovereignty," respectively.
Since these primary meanings are precluded in this context, the words *mugdha* and others indicate [the smile and other expressions] through the cause of their similarity to those primary meanings.
And he says "mugdha" and so forth to show that by means of that [smile], a particular excellence of beauty and the like is revealed;
"mugdhamadhura" and so forth— this means that "mugdha," "madhura," and the others are the primary meanings.
"Completely set aside" means that they are sublated;
this is the intended sense.
The word "by them" is connected with the phrase "being suggested."

Here, according to the respective order [of the qualities], by that [smile] there is the unextracted, unartificial beauty of the smile; of the gaze, the quality of being beloved by all people and its inexhaustible range;
and of the speech, the quality of pacifying distress and its capacity to satisfy.

The meaning is that, by virtue of her gait being produced by delicate feet, its slowness and its constant persistence as a graceful playfulness are suggested, as well as the fact that her youth is endowed with a state desirable even with effort;
this is to be connected with the phrase "being a vessel for other qualities" (*dharmāntarapātratā*).
The meaning is: being a vessel for other qualities such as beauty that have not been acquired [by others].
"Sthavira-vedhāḥ" refers to Brahmā.
"Tat" (that) refers to...
The meaning is "a vessel for smiles.
The word "iti" indicates a reason.
Regarding the phrase "in all cases," and so forth:
The meaning is that this should be understood in all cases.
"Only novelty appears" refers to the smiles and so forth in the passage beginning with "an impending delusion."
To whom are these passionate women not dear— those with tremulous eyes, faltering speech, and the breaking forth of playful smiles, who move slowly due to the weight of their hips?
Even though there exist verses such as these, through the reliance on *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is set aside (*tiraskṛtavācya*), a state of unprecedentedness (*apūrvatva*) alone manifests.
For example: "He who is the first is truly the first; for he is a lion among the hosts of beasts of prey, devouring the abundant flesh of slain elephants. By whom can a lion be surpassed?"
By whom else can his greatness, purchased by his own splendor, be surpassed?
Is a lion ever overcome even by great elephants?
In such verses as these, even though they exist, there is novelty by virtue of relying on *dhvani* where the expressed meaning is transferred (*saṅkramitavācya*).

There is also novelty for that in which the expressed meaning is intended but subordinate (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*) by relying on the aforementioned modes—as, for example: "Having placed her face upon the face of her lover, who was feigning sleep, the young woman remained with her eyes fixed on his expansive chest, eager for enjoyment, though the passion for the kiss was checked by her fear of being discovered."
The connection is that "the eye" implies "freshness.
In the second case, the word "first" manifests its own primary meaning as it has shifted toward other suggested qualities (*vyaṅgyadharma*), such as being unassailable, preeminence, or uniqueness.
Likewise, the word "lion" also resonates with its own primary meaning as it has shifted toward other suggested qualities, such as heroism, independence, or wonderfulness.
Having thus illustrated two varieties of the first [type], he provides a preliminary outline for illustrating the second as well, beginning with the words "vivakṣita" (intended).
In the state of sleep, "kaitavī" means feigned sleep. "Vinyasya vadane vaktram" means having placed his face upon her face.
She is not even able to abandon the divine pleasure born merely from the touch of his face; for this very reason, he is called "the beloved. The term *vadhū* refers to a newly married bride.

The meaning is that, although [the smile] was forcibly suppressed out of fear of awakening— that is, out of fear of waking her beloved— it somehow, somehow proceeded; and even when describing the four [types of smiles], the fact that the description of this particular one is unprecedented shines forth in such passages as "a slight smile" (kiñcit-smita).
The same should be understood for what follows as well.

"Anapeti" means that in which there exists another property (*dharmāntara*) whose nature is characterized by being non-departing, not requiring removal, preeminence, uniqueness, and so forth; this is the meaning.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "vīratva" (heroism) and so forth should also be understood in this way. Regarding "kṛtaka," it means "deceptive."
"Tāvat" means "in the beginning. "Pārayati" means [he brings to completion].
The word "bride" (vadhū) is to be supplied [as the subject]. Regarding the word "iti," the word "was manifested" (vyajyata) is to be supplied.
"From this very fact" means: from the fact of producing such joy.
"Thus" means: [as follows].
The meaning is "it has been said thus.
By stating that [the mind] is restrained, he expresses what is implied: "even though proceeding by force.

[Thinking], "He may turn away out of embarrassment," [the lover acts]. Thus, for that one who has ceased his efforts, the heart—characterized by a lingering expectation—reaches the further shore of delight.
Regarding this verse and others:
Having observed that the bedchamber was empty, she rose slightly and slowly from her bed; she gazed for a long time at the face of her husband, who had feigned sleep.
Trustingly kissing him, she saw his cheeks covered in horripilation; with her face bowed in shame, the young girl was kissed for a long time by her laughing beloved.
Even though such verses exist, there is still novelty.
Or, for example: "She whose eyes, with the knitting of their brows like waves, held a desire to kiss for but a moment;
therefore, she remained having made them tremulous by repeatedly opening them wide to observe and gaze upon her sleep."

The meaning is that she is not able to turn away from kissing altogether. [This is said] regarding her beloved, who has desisted from the act of kissing, thinking: "If she, being in such a state, is kissed by me, she will become embarrassed and turn her face away."

"The heart is that which possesses a longing for attainment. This means its state of being is one characterized by a longing—that is, a yearning—such that it is distressed by a thirst for blood (or a craving for union), rather than having its purpose fulfilled by the attainment of its desires.

However, it has reached the further shore of a supreme bliss (*paranirvṛti*) consisting of the pride that regards each other as the very essence of life, a bliss whose depths have not been fathomed by any other experience; thus, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is indeed brought to full completion.
In the second verse, however, the mutual kissing has been accomplished and her bashfulness is expressed by its own name; thus,
although the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) is indeed nourished by that as well,
it was nonetheless obstructed in the first verse by the impossibility of reaching the culmination of the successive stages of the expansion of mutual longing.
Intending that the term *bhoga* signifies direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*), he says: "by means of manifestation," and so forth.
Regarding "sleep": the meaning is that it is the observation or perception which consists of the investigation of sleep through the cognition, "This one is sleeping."
By this, the re-emergence of the desire for a kiss is understood.
Having made it tremulous, in such a way as to be accompanied by doubt regarding the kiss;
he states the intended meaning with the words "but not," and so forth.
He explains the second half [of the verse] with the words "In this way," and so forth.
"Vilakṣā" means being ashamed. "Iti" is used in the sense of a reason.
The word *api* serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the bride. *Ruharuhi-kākadarthitaṃ* means tormented by longing.
He states the intended meaning (*gamyārtha*) with the words beginning "but not," and so forth.
In some manuscripts, the reading "yadyapi" (even though) appears immediately after "caritārtham" (its purpose having been fulfilled); however, that is an explanation of the word "nāma" (namely).
The word "kintu" (but), on the other hand, expresses the meaning of the particle "tu" (but/rather).
"By experience" means by the experience of kissing, embracing, and so forth. "Unobtained" [means...]
The meaning is "in that [ocean] wherein immersion has not been attained.
Although there is an apparent contradiction in saying "one has reached the further shore" when immersion has not even been attained,
he says "the second verse," and so forth, in order to demonstrate the novelty of this verse.
He raises an objection with "by that too," etc.;
he provides a resolution with "even so," etc.;
[and the term] "mutually."

The sequence of cessations of the mutual flow of desire—that which is its culmination—and so forth, constitutes the distinctness [of this verse] from the verse beginning with "the earth wandering in various ways" (*nānābhaṅgibhramadbhūḥ*).
By means of this reasoning, the extensive range of *rasa* and the like is to be pursued;
for it is by relying upon this that the path of poetry attains mutual infinitude. (Dhvanyāloka 4.3)
By this method, the extensive range of sentiments (*rasa*) and other elements should be pursued;
for it is by relying upon this that the path of poetry attains mutual infinity. (3)

This path, characterized by rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), and their pacification, is very extensive according to the respective distinctions of the excitants (vibhāva) and ensuants (anubhāva), as previously stated.
All of this is to be followed by means of this method;

for this path of poetry, being the locus of rasa and the other elements, attains mutual infinity through its manifold varieties, having been thoroughly traversed in many ways by thousands or even countless ancient poets.

For each of the sentiments (*rasa*), emotional states (*bhāva*), and so forth, there is an infinite variety due to their respective dependence upon determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory mental states (*vyabhicārin*).

Even with respect to a single sub-division of these, the course of the world as depicted by skilled poets turns out quite differently from how it actually exists, according to the power of their creative will.
This has already been established in the section examining the marvelous (*citramīmāṃsā*).
Locana is said to be Rati;
by indicating that she enters into the same nature of the mental state as both [the hero and the heroine], she further nourishes Rati. // 2 // // //

Having thus illustrated the four primary varieties, he provides a definition covering all sub-varieties by means of extension to the varieties where the sequence is unperceived (*alakṣyakrama*): "One should apply [this] by means of logic";
that is to say, "it should be followed" (or "it should be illustrated").
As it has been said:
"The various divisions of its members, as well as the internal subdivisions themselves— the conceptualization of their mutual relationship is infinite."
In this regard,
it has been established;
the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "api" (also) and its position in the sequence is displaced.
This too is "dear to the ignorant" (bālapriya); the meaning is "without its possibility," that is, without the possibility of that [attainment]. "Rati" means "nirvṛti" (blissful cessation).
"Ukta" means "shown.
"Sutarām" means "all the more so."
The meaning is that it is far more than what is stated in the second verse. // 2 // // //
"The four primary divisions" means as follows:

there are two divisions of *avivakṣitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is not intended), namely *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (where the expressed meaning is completely set aside) and *saṅkramitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is transferred);

and there are two divisions of *vivakṣitānyaparavācya* (where the expressed meaning is intended but has another [primary] purpose), namely *asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is of imperceptible sequence) and *saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is of perceptible sequence). This is the meaning of the "four primary divisions."

By the phrase "having cited," it is made clear that the verse beginning with *taraṅga* (from the *Vikramorvaśīya*) is an example of suggestion where the sequence [of the process] is perceptible (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya*).
As for that verse cited in the second chapter (*udyota*), it is as follows: [and] how it serves as an example thereof.
Thus it should be considered by those with discerning hearts.
The verse beginning with "nānābhaṅgī" has not been found in its entirety. [The commentary continues: "alakṣya... etc.

The meaning is "among the intermediate subdivisions of the [suggestion] where the sequence is imperceptible. The explanation of the word *anusartavya* ("to be followed") found in the verse is *udāhartavya* ("to be illustrated").
The phrase *tasyāṅgānām* ("of its limbs," etc. is the statement of the referent of the word *prāk* ("previously") in the expression *yathoktaṃ prāk* ("as stated before").
"The meaning of the word 'api' (also/even)" means "conjunction" (samuccaya).
The connection [of the sentence] is that this has been established in this context.
Regarding the phrase "not abiding as such," he completes the sense with the word "outside.
This means "the world outside the heart.
And on this point, a verse has already been composed by the Great Poet:

That speech which, though not placed there, settles within the heart as if it were already situated there regarding a particular meaning— that speech is victorious, having the power to pierce through all obstacles.
Victorious is that speech, the domain of the formidable poet, which places within the heart specific meanings— even those not existing as such— making them appear as if they were so situated.
[Thus ends the *chāyā*].
In this way, the infinity of the meanings of poetry based on rasa, bhāva, and so forth has been well demonstrated.

To further substantiate this very point, it is said in the *Locana*: "It was established [in the previous section] that 'even non-sentient things are like sentient beings, and sentient things are like non-sentient beings.'"
"Even though they do not exist as such, they appear externally as if so situated"—
by the word "as if" (iva), the meaning is that because there is an absence of resting in either [of the two states], they are all the more of a variegated nature. "In the heart" (hṛdaye).
The meaning is: in that which is most preeminent, the touchstone for the gold of all states of being.
"He establishes" means that he causes each and every person who possesses a heart to remain there with immovability.
Thus, these particular meanings result as something entirely distinct from those meanings well-known [in common usage].
And the meaning is that they exist only as they are when fixed within the heart, and not otherwise.
That [speech] triumphs; it exists with superiority even over the Prajāpatis whose powers are limited.
By his grace alone, the subject matter to be described, which falls within the domain of the poet, becomes vast and boundless. // 3 //

Regarding what was stated previously—that the infinity of inspired expressions and utterances is brought about by *dhvani*—that very point is now established through a specific method (*bhaṅgyā*) by means of a verse (*kārikā*). Thus he says: "in order to demonstrate" (*upapādayitum*).
The meaning is: "to establish by means of reasoning" (*upapattyā*).
The sense is that although the author of the *Vṛtti* stated "the mere infinity of objects" as the reason, it was not stated by the author of the *Kārikā*.
Alternatively, the sense is that this is stated as a summary verse (*saṃgrahaśloka*).
For this very reason, no commentary was provided for this verse in the Vṛtti text;
the intention is that [it was not explained] by means of the word "iva" (like),
which signifies a possibility (*sambhāvanā*).
The meaning is as follows:
the word "is understood" (*gamyate*) is to be supplied.
[Regarding] "entire" (*samasta*):
The meaning is that all things (*samastabhāvāḥ*), that is, all objects (*sakalapadārthāḥ*), are the gold, and [the Guru] is the touchstone for them.
The phrase "he places [it] within the heart" is explained by the words beginning with "of whom" (*yasya*).
Precisely for this reason, that is, solely because of its placement within the heart.
These are the meanings established in the heart.
The explanation of the phrase "particulars of meaning" (*arthaviśeṣānitya*) begins with "well-known" (*prasiddha*), and so forth. "In that way" (*tathā*).

The meaning is "particular meanings. Intending the etymological derivation as "that whose range is the domain of poets" (*vikaṭaḥ kavigocaro yasyāḥ*), he explains it with the words "the domain of poets," and so forth. // 3 // // //
He introduces the passage beginning with "etadeva" (this very [point]) with the words "pratibhānām" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "dhvanikṛtam":
it means produced by the infinity of meanings resulting from the various types of *dhvani* (suggested meaning).
"Unexpounded" means not clearly manifest due to the lack of an explanation of its logical derivation;
"stated" means... [text continues].
The meaning is that this was stated by [the author] beginning with the words "dhvaneḥ ya" (of the resonance, which...).
Regarding the phrase "stated by the commentator" (vṛttikāreṇokta),
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "on the occasion of explaining the verse beginning with 'yuktyānayā'."
Regarding the term *saṃgrahaśloka*:
it means a transitional verse (*parikaraśloka*) composed by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*).
For even objects previously perceived [become distinct] through the inclusion of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in poetry.
All appear as if new, like trees in the month of honey (spring).
For even objects previously seen appear as if entirely new in poetry due to the absorption of aesthetic flavor (rasa), just as trees do in the month of spring.

For instance, novelty arises precisely from the recourse to that type of suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*)—which consists of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) produced by the power of words (*śabdaśakti*)—in the case of *anyapara-vācya* (where the expressed sense is subordinate to another).
As in the example: "Now you, O Śeṣa, are the bearer of the earth," and so forth.
[The full verse is: "Śeṣa, the Himālaya mountain, and you are all great, venerable, and steadfast."
For they uphold the earth as it moves, even though its boundaries have been transgressed.

Even though such [other figures] exist, this [poetry] possesses novelty by relying on a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) that takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) arising from the power of the sense (*arthaśakti*).
For example, as in the verse beginning with "When the divine sage spoke thus... (*evaṃvādini devarṣau*).
When an excellent conversation has been held, the young maidens,
their faces bowed down with inward bashfulness, indicate their longing through the bristling of their hair.

In such cases as these, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which takes the form of a resonance arising from the power of the sense (*artha-śakti-udbhava*), possesses novelty because its body is constructed through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet;
as, for example,
in "The spring season prepares itself" (*sajjei surahimāso*) and so forth.
When the season of fragrances has arrived, delightful longings arise suddenly in those possessed by passion, along with the buds of the *sahakāra* tree.
Even though such [examples] exist, there is indeed a state of being unprecedented (*apūrvatva*).

Because the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), which arises as a resonance produced by the power of the sense (*arthaśaktyudbhava*), possesses a novel quality (*navatva*) in that its body is accomplished solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker composed by the poet, [it is considered new].
Locana: "Seen before" (*dṛṣṭapūrvā*).
This is to be understood in two ways: externally through means of valid cognition such as direct perception, and [internally] through the words of ancient poets.
Poetry stands in the place of honey and meat; it is "desire" and "shame," and for those possessed by passion, it is "itching."
What charm can there be in a meaning that has already been touched upon by words?

These examples have already been explained in detail previously; so what is the point of repeating them? Even though they were touched upon by earlier poets, they certainly attain novelty through the favor of this particular method—this is the sole intent of the work, and nothing more.
He explains the meaning connected with the word *druma* (tree) starting with "outside" (*bahiḥ*), etc.;
he explains the meaning connected with the word *artha* (wealth/purpose) starting with "by former ones" (*prāktanaiḥ*), etc.;
and [he asks] "what is the charm? (*kā hṛdyatā*).

Therefore, the meaning is that there is novelty [in the poem] starting from the verse beginning with "kṛta," continuing through the verse beginning with "evaṃvādinī," then the verse beginning with "surabhī," and finally the verse beginning with "sajjati. Regarding the phrase "even though [they are]," the word "of these" (eteṣām) is to be supplied as the remainder.
The connection is that novelty indeed arises from favoring this type [of expression],
as in the meaning of the verse beginning with "O merchant, women's teeth... and so forth.
My son is like a female elephant in his eagerness for battle; he can strike down with a single arrow, carrying a quiver so full that it seems as if it were overflowing with arrows.
"My son, who brought widowhood upon female elephants by striking them with a single arrow,
has been treated by his slain daughter-in-law in such a way that he now carries a quiver of arrows."
[Thus the shadow.
Even when such meanings exist, there is simply no contact [with them].
Just as the novelty of the meanings of poetry arises through the manifestation of the various types of the suggested (vyaṅgya) within Dhvani, so too [is it here].
Likewise, this also applies by relying on the distinction between the manifestors (*vyañjaka*).
However, that is not written here for fear of excessive prolixity; it should be inferred by the discerning (*sahṛdaya*) themselves.
Furthermore, although it has been stated repeatedly, this is said once more because of its essential importance:
Although this relationship between the manifested and the manifestor can occur in various ways,
the poet should apply his attention specifically to that which consists of rasa and the like.
Although this manifold relationship between the suggested and the suggester is possible,
the poet should apply his focused attention specifically to that single instance which consists of rasa and the like.

Although a manifold variety of words is possible within this relationship of the manifested (*vyaṅgya*) and the manifestor (*vyañjaka*), which is the cause for the infinity of meaning, a poet seeking the attainment of unprecedented meaning should apply effort toward a single relationship of the manifested and the manifestor consisting of rasa and the like.

For when the manifested takes the form of rasa, bhāva, or their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and the manifestors consist of the aforementioned phonemes, words, sentences, compositions, and literary works, everything becomes unprecedented poetry for the poet whose mind is attentive.
And likewise, although battles and other such events are recounted again and again in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the *Mahābhārata*, and so forth, they appear ever new.
Furthermore, when only a single dominant sentiment (*rasa*) is portrayed in a literary composition, it nourishes a specific excellence of meaning and an extraordinary brilliance.
If one asks "In what [work]?"—it is as in the *Rāmāyaṇa* or as in the *Mahābhārata*.

For in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, the sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*) was indeed sown by the Primordial Poet himself when he spoke thus: "Grief has attained the state of verse. And that very sentiment was brought to its full fruition; my son, who was capable of bringing about the widowhood of the female elephant (Karṇī) with a single arrow, was treated by his slain daughter-in-law in such a way that he carries the arrow as the instrument [of his own death], so that the literal meaning of the verse remains untouched—this is the connection. // 4 //

In the *Bālapriyā*, the phrase "of this kind" (*etatprakāra*) means "of the varieties of suggestion" (*dhvaniprabheda*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*), regarding the expression "freshness by way of its body," the word "exists" (*bhavati*) is to be supplied as the remainder in both instances. "Falling with a single arrow" (*ekakāṇḍavinipātī*) is the literal rendering (*chāyā*);
its explanation is "by a single arrow," and so forth.
Kāṇḍa means an arrow. // 4 //
By composing his own work with the ultimate separation from Sītā as its conclusion,
and likewise by concluding even the *Mahābhārata*— which, though a scripture, possesses the shadow of poetry— with a finale that bestows despondency through the bitter end of the Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas,
the Great Sage primarily intended for his own composition the purpose of engendering dispassion (*vairāgya*).
By demonstrating this, the human goal characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*) and the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*) have been indicated as the primary objects of his intention.
And this has indeed been explained by other commentators;

it was proclaimed by the Lord of the World himself, who, desiring to uplift the world submerged in the great delusion of existence, bestowed the light of exceedingly pure knowledge: "In whatever way the worldly course proceeds, being devoid of essence..."
In that very way, detachment arises here; of this there is no doubt.
By using the term "atyanta" (absolute), Locana dispels the suspicion of deception through its state of being independent.
There is the mutual destruction of the Vṛṣṇis,
and for the Pāṇḍavas as well, an undeserved calamity resulting from the hardships of the great journey.
Even for Kṛṣṇa, there was destruction at the hands of a hunter; thus, the end of everything is indeed devoid of essence (*virasa*).
Regarding the phrase "primarily" (*mukhyatayā*): although it has been stated that [he is the authority] "in dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa,"...

Nevertheless, the four *cakāras* speak thus: "Even though there is nothing among *dharma*, *artha*, and *kāma* that does not exist elsewhere, nevertheless, let the ultimate insipidity of these very things be observed here;
and as for the nature of *mokṣa*, let its essence be investigated right here."
Regarding the phrase "in whatever way":
although things characterized as dharma, artha, kāma, and their means— which are strung together by the world and accomplished with effort— are regarded as real entities,
[they are seen] through various modes such as acquisition, preservation, and depletion.
It is deceptive, like a hollow conjurer’s trick; on the contrary,
it turns out to be the opposite.

The meaning is that let alone the consideration of its essential nature (*svarūpa*); by the phrase "dispassion arises here in this worldly system" (*lokatantre*) in various ways, [the author] states the purpose of including the word "absolute" (*atyanta*) in the expression "until the absolute separation from Sītā" (*sītātyantaviyogaparyantam*), namely: "by the inclusion of the word 'absolute'... and so forth. *Bālapriyā* [comments]: "Let alone the consideration of its essential nature" means that the inquiry into its true form is set aside. By the statement "dispassion arises here in this worldly system" in various modes, [he indicates] the world-weariness (*nirveda*) born from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). [He then explains] the result of including the term "absolute" (*atyanta*) in the phrase "until the absolute separation from Sītā. He says: "By the inclusion of the word 'absolute'... and so on.

Regarding the statement "it was said that it ends with the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis and Pāṇḍavas," [the author] says "of the Vṛṣṇis," and so forth. Having raised the objection that what was stated— that the human goal characterized by liberation (mokṣa) is indicated as the primary subject of the intended discourse— is untenable, he refutes it with the words beginning "even though" (yadyapi).
And it has been stated regarding liberation:
"In some ancient text, O bull of the Bharatas, the reading is: 'What is found here is found elsewhere; what is not found here is found nowhere.
Thus they say.
The meaning is that they illuminate the specific distinction that is about to be stated.
"The whole self" (sarvasva) means the primary essential nature.
"It does not exist"—the word "here" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. The connection is: that which is not found elsewhere does not exist here in such a manner.
The sense is that what exists here also exists elsewhere.
He shows the specific point to be illustrated with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) and so forth.
[This refers to] the state of being ultimately insipid (*paryantavirasatva*).
The terms "dharma, artha, and kāma" are to be supplied [to the verse]. He explains the phrase "worldly conduct" (*lokatantra*) with the words "by worldly people," and so forth;
thus he speaks at great length.

Consequently, it is very clearly evident that the intended meaning of the *Mahābhārata* is that the peaceful sentiment (*śānta-rasa*), characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*), which is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), is the primary element (*aṅgin*) when it is pursued as such, while other human goals are pursued as its subordinates. And the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) among the sentiments has already been demonstrated accordingly.
With respect to the ultimate internal reality, it is not contradictory for even the *rasa*—which is subordinate to the body—as well as the *puruṣārtha*, to possess beauty through their own primacy.
Now, one might object: "In the *Mahābhārata*, whatever was intended as the subject matter has all been enumerated in the *Anukramaṇī*; yet this [beauty] is not seen there.
On the contrary, in that enumeration, it is understood through the explicit words themselves that the *Mahābhārata* is the cause for awakening to all *puruṣārthas* and contains all *rasas*."

To this it is replied: It is true that in the *Mahābhārata*, the sentiment of tranquility (*śānta-rasa*) alone is the predominant element and liberation (*mokṣa*) is the most primary among all human goals; however, this is not shown by the table of contents (*anukramaṇī*) through direct verbal expression, but rather as an implied meaning (*vyaṅgya*). This is evident in the statement: "And the eternal Lord Vāsudeva is celebrated herein.

For by this sentence, the following meaning is intended as an implication: that whatever account of the Pāṇḍavas and others is celebrated here in the *Mahābhārata* is entirely devoid of ultimate flavor and is of the nature of the phenomenal expansion of ignorance (*avidyā-prapañca*).

But it is the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, whose very nature is the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya), who is celebrated here. Therefore, direct your cultivated minds toward that Supreme Lord alone; do not become attached to His manifestations, which are devoid of essence, nor let your intellects be entirely fixed upon these mere qualities—such as statesmanship, discipline, and valor—nor upon any of them individually.

And likewise, further on: "Behold the worthlessness of saṃsāra"—by indicating this very meaning through the *locana* (commentary) which points to the *śānta-rasa* as the stable emotion (*sthāyin*), its preeminence is declared by establishing that it alone is the essence while all else is worthless. Now, one might object: "But does not the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) of the *śṛṅgāra*, *vīra*, and other rasas also appear there? Anticipating this, he says: "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*).
For those who are intent on enjoyment and possessed by worldly tendencies (*lokavāsanā*), such a conceit arises even toward a rasa that has become merely a subordinate element (*aṅga*).

Just as the conceit of being a knower (*pramātṛtva-abhimāna*) exists in the body, even though it is merely the locus of experience for the knower, so too [does it exist] in the instruments of devotion to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-bhakty-upakaraṇeṣu*). "As real entities" (*vastubhūtatayā*) means "as ultimate reality" (*paramārthatayā*).
"Empty" means empty,
such as a hare's horn and so forth;
"of that very [thing]" refers to that.
The meaning is "of the *śānta* rasa alone.
He introduces the passage beginning with "pāramārthika" by saying "nanu" and so forth.
In that regard, [it is stated] in the *Mahābhārata*:
He explains the state [of being] with the words beginning "enjoyment" (bhoga) and so forth.
"Such conceit" means the conceit of preeminence.
The connection is that this applies even to the body, which is merely a material thing (mātra).
The word, assisted by the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā-śakti*), shines forth as clearly illuminating [this meaning].
The subsequent verses, beginning with "For he is the Truth" (*sa hi satyam*), are seen to demonstrate this very kind of meaning held within [the word].

And this deeply hidden yet beautiful meaning was perfectly clarified by that very creator of poets, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, who brought the *Mahābhārata* to its conclusion with the description of the *Harivaṃśa*.

And by this very meaning, which instills an excellence of devotion toward the ultimate reality that transcends *saṃsāra*, the entire worldly convention is set forth as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and is revealed in its full detail.
This includes the various deities such as those associated with sacred sites (*tīrtha*) and asceticism (*tapas*), as well as others;

even the description of the life-stories of the Pāṇḍavas and so forth has the purpose of generating detachment (*vairāgya*). Since detachment is the root of liberation (*mokṣa*), and since liberation is primarily shown in the *Gītā* and other scriptures to be the means for attaining the Blessed Lord, it follows that [the aforementioned descriptions] serve exclusively as means for attaining the Supreme Brahman.

The Supreme Brahman, which is the locus of immeasurable power and is designated by names such as Vāsudeva through traditional succession— having attained renown in other passages of the Gītā and elsewhere as being denoted by those very terms— is intended here as having its entire nature manifested in the Mathurā incarnation; it is not intended merely as the partial manifestation at Mathurā alone.
Because it is qualified by the word "eternal" (sanātana).
The meaning of "but not the eye" (locanam tu) is that there is no fault.
The connection is: "May those who are attached to manifestations (vibhūti) and whose intellects are fixed upon the qualities (guṇa) [not be so]."

The word "agra" (beginning) means in that Bhārata text which follows the table of contents (*anukramaṇī*). Now, one might object: "Vāsudeva is said to be the offspring of Vasudeva, not the Supreme Lord, the Supreme Self, Mahādeva. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by being denoted by such names as Vāsudeva and so forth."
"At the end of many births, the man of knowledge resorts to Me,
[realizing] Vāsudeva is everything"— the *Bālapriyā* commentary shows the sequence with the words "among the manifestations" (*vibhūtiṣu*) and so forth;
and in the *Vṛtti*, it says "and thus" (*tathā ca*) and so forth.
The connection is that the word appears while illuminating; "in its entirety" (anyakṣeṇa) means "completely" (kārtsnyena).
The syntactical connection is that [the text] describes [them] as means for attainment (*prāptyupāya*).
In the phrase "of the specific deities" (*devatāviśeṣāṇām*), the description of their superior power (*prabhāvātiśaya*) is to be supplied. Regarding the word "of liberation" (*mokṣasya*):
The meaning is "due to the cessation of ignorance.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that Brahman is intended to be expressed by the name "Vāsudeva.
"By being its designation" means "by being expressible through the name Vāsudeva."
That by which the entire essential nature is imitated through that manifestation which is Māthura;
[this refers to the phrase] "but not," and so forth. The word "intended" (*vivakṣita*) is to be construed with this [phrase] *viparimāṇām*.
He states another reason as well: "In the Rāmāyaṇa and so forth," and so on.
The term "human purpose" (puruṣārtha) is connected with the word "intended" (vivakṣita).
This is because, in the Rāmāyaṇa and other such works, we observe the use of this designation for other forms of the Blessed One.
And this point has been definitively established by those who know the true nature of words.

Thus, it has been well demonstrated that by means of the statement indicated in the *Anukramaṇī*, which reveals the impermanence of everything other than the Blessed One, it is intended—in the perspective of the Śāstra—that the single supreme human goal characterized by liberation (*mokṣa*) is the primary theme;

and in the perspective of poetry (*kāvyanyāya*), it is intended that the *śānta* rasa, characterized by the nourishment of the bliss of the extinction of craving, is the principal element of the *Mahābhārata*.

Furthermore, because it constitutes the ultimate essence, this meaning is shown only as the suggested (vyaṅgya) and not as the expressed (vācya). For an essential meaning shines forth all the more when it is manifested by not being denotable by its own words. And this is indeed a well-known convention in the assemblies of refined scholars: that an object most highly desired is revealed through suggestion, rather than by being directly expressed by words.
In passages such as "locanam," the intended meaning has been determined to be that this [term] is denoted by its own name in the form of its constituent parts (*aṃśi*).
Regarding the phrase "and it has been determined":
it was stated in the rule “ṛṣy-andhaka-vṛṣṇi-kurubhyaś-ca” that words, being indeed eternal, are subsequently designated in such a manner through the principle of "coincidence" (*kākatālīya*).

Regarding the phrase "the system of the treatise" (*śāstranaya*): the intention is that in the absence of the application of aesthetic relish (*āsvādayoga*), the designation "that which is sought by a person" (*puruṣeṇārthyate*) is used with due respect; however, when there is the application of wonder (*camatkāra*), the designation "rasa" is employed.
And this has been stated by the author [Abhayākaragupta] in his *Tattvāloka* after careful consideration; however, since this is not the primary occasion for it here, we have not demonstrated it.
Regarding what was said—"all the more so"—he states the reason for that: "and because it is well-known.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*).
Since this worldly convention is beginningless, even the Blessed Vyāsa and others had precisely this intention when employing the term *asva* (horse);

for otherwise, what proof would there be that the Blessed One’s intention was likewise [to use the term] in such a manner when defining the meaning of words in contexts such as the relationship between action and its factors, or in passages like "having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa"? This is the underlying sense.
By the mention of "learned and discerning scholars," the path of poetry (*kāvyanyāya*) and the path of the treatises (*śāstranyāya*) have been followed.

Having stated that "the poet should be attentive toward this [work] which consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth," he now concludes that very point after the incidental discussion regarding its connection to the *Mahābhārata*: "Therefore, it is established."
In the *Locana*, [the author] explains the passage beginning with "in other places such as those where songs are sung" by saying "of many," and so forth.
"By way of the 'crow-and-palm' principle" (*kākatālīya*) means "by chance.
This is to be connected with the phrase "it has been stated here."

The phrase "in the Kāśikāvṛtti" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. He explains what was stated— that in the system of the Śāstra, liberation (mokṣa) is the human goal (puruṣārtha), whereas in the system of poetry (kāvyanyaya), the peaceful sentiment (śāntarasa) is so— by saying "therein," and so forth.
"Sādara" means "worthy"; that is the meaning. "Yasmāt" means "because."
The meaning is that it has the sense of "the cause.
"This very one" means precisely that which is well-known among assemblies of clever and learned people.

Regarding the expression "not by its own word" (*asvaśabdābhidhāne*): when the intended object is not expressed by its own word, the "intention" (*āśaya*) is the intended reason. He states the supporting argument for this with the words "otherwise," and so forth.

In verses such as "Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa," the intended connection of the word *nārāyaṇa* and others with the act of salutation through a relationship such as that of action and agent is what is meant.
Thus, the intended connection of the words *nārāyaṇa* and so forth with the act of salutation through a relationship such as that of action and agent is what is meant.

Likewise, the meanings of the words *nārāyaṇa* and others—such as Viṣṇu—and the intention behind them [are established]. Therefore, this is settled: when a poem is composed based on a dominant aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and its like, there arises a new acquisition of meaning, which constitutes the "beauty of composition" (*bandhacchāyā*).
And thus it becomes great.

For this very reason, even in the absence of other poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), a composition that employs specific meanings suited to the sentiment (*rasa*) is seen in actual literary works to possess an excellence of aesthetic luster (*chāyātiśaya*).
As, for example: "Victorious is the sage, the lord of yogis, the great-souled one born from a water-jar (Agastya)."
By means of which those two divine fish and tortoises were seen in a single mouthful.
In such passages as this,
the sight of fish and tortoises within a single drinking bowl (culaka), being consistent with the sentiment of the marvelous (adbhuta-rasa), nourishes an excellence of aesthetic charm (chāyātiśaya).

For there, even though the entire ocean is present within that single bowl, the sight of divine fish and tortoises is more perfectly suited to the marvelous sentiment because it remains unimpaired [by the constraints of reality].
For this reason, the object is indeed "crushed" by the eye;
since it stands thus, therefore even that which is seen in the object of perception is established, whereas otherwise it would be entirely untenable.
Nor is that [beauty] untenable,
because it is perceived as such; the intention is that the very cause of this is precisely its being meaningful in accordance with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
Regarding the phrase "another ornament" (*alaṅkārāntara*):
the word *antara* denotes a distinction.
Alternatively, since the ornament *rasavat* is present in the example intended to be cited, the term "another ornament" is used in relation to that.

One might object: "Is it not the case that the proximity of the ocean perceived from the sight of fish and turtles in a single cup leads to the realization of the sage's majesty? Therefore, the suggested meaning (pratīyamāna) is not nourished by a literal meaning (vācya) that conforms to the rasa. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For here... One might further object: "In that case, let the perception of the ocean itself be what conforms to the wonder (adbhuta); thus, the expressed meaning (vācya) here is the one that conforms to the rasa. How then can this be an example [of the suggested meaning nourishing the rasa]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Therein..."
The word "kṣuṇṇam" (trampled) means that because it has been repeatedly described, examined, and so forth, its nature is utterly worn away by being ground down like flour; that is the meaning.
Furthermore, the sense is that this [definition] is "bālapriyā," meaning it conforms to worldly convention and is thus applicable to a vast number of instances.
He explains the passage beginning with "for this very reason" and ending with "is seen" as follows: "since," etc.
"Of that" means:
because of its being perceived as beautiful.
Regarding the phrase "even in the absence of another ornament," he explains the term "another ornament" in two ways—beginning with "the word 'another ornament'... and so forth.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason.
"Na" and so forth [follows].
However, the intended meaning is that the *chāyā* (shadow or suggestion) is nourished precisely by the aforementioned *vyaṅgya* (suggested sense).
In the commentary, it says: "consonant with the marvelous sentiment (*adbhutarasa*).
This means it is consonant with the marvelous sentiment based upon the sage.
"By way of the 'crow-and-palm' principle" (*kākatālīyena*) is an explanation of the sense of the term *bhāva*.
"'Attached' (*pratilagna*)" means a connection with the side of the hero.
The indeclinable *asī* is used in the sense of "you.
O fortunate one, the construction is as follows: "By which side you passed her, that side of hers, clinging to the tip of the balance-beam, is even today perspiring," and so forth.
Regarding the word "paraspara" (mutual):
the sense is that because the passion residing in the hero is perceived through the transgression of the connection with his side [the heroine],
it is not surprising even though it is extraordinary according to worldly convention.

Furthermore, a subject matter that has not been previously experienced (*akṣuṇṇa*) when employed is suitable not only for the marvelous sentiment (*adbhutarasā*), but even for other sentiments as well.
For example: "He perspires, his hair stands on end, and he trembles, having caught hold of the edge of the street-cloth;
O handsome one, even today he is still bound by the noose because you have passed him by."

The aesthetic realization (*rasapratīti*) that arises from contemplating the meaning of this verse does not arise even slightly from such implied meanings as "she perspires upon touching you," "her hair stands on end," or "she trembles.
Thus, it has been demonstrated how the novelty of poetic meanings is produced by relying on the various divisions of *dhvani*.

Even for that which is suggested as a subordinate element (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*), novelty in poetic subjects certainly arises by relying on those modes that exist in relation to the three types of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Since this would result in an excessive expansion [of the text], it has not been illustrated here; rather, it should be envisioned by the connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*) themselves.
The *Locana* demonstrates this with the words beginning "And not... (*na ca...*).
"By chance, on the street, he was caught by the tip of the scale; O fortunate one, that side of hers by which he passed is still [visible] today.
This refers to the "perception of rasa," meaning the perception of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) where the causes are mutually dependent.
He confirms that this meaning is consistent with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) by means of a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), beginning with the words "She [the Goddess] you... and so forth.
At the commencement of the *Udyota*, there is a verse stating: "The path of *dhvani* which possesses subordinated suggestion (*saguṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) has been demonstrated.

Therein, the portion explaining how the infinite quality of the poets' creative intuition (*pratibhā*) becomes the path of *dhvani* has been commented upon; he concludes this with the words "Thus, in this manner... and so forth.
He explains the portion beginning with "saguṇībhūtavyaṅgyasya" by means of the words "guṇībhūta... and so forth.

The meaning is: by that dependence upon the expressed (vācya) which consists in the subordination (guṇībhāva) of the suggested (vyaṅgya)—which is threefold, having the nature of matter (vastu), ornament (alaṅkāra), and aesthetic flavor (rasa).
In that regard, since all the varieties of dhvani are infinite due to their subordination, he says: "because of the extreme extensiveness."
Regarding the word "svayam" (itself):

therein, by means of the object (*vastu*) which is suggested (*vyaṅgya*) yet subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), there is novelty (*navatvam*) even when there is contact with an old meaning. For example, as in my own [verse]: "For those who have come for refuge, seeking protection from the dangers of existence, it is only right that no opportunity for rest was granted to them, even for a mere moment.
In this case, although the sense of "it is only right" (*yuktam idam*) is already established by the context, its novelty arises through the specific manner in which the object is presented.

In this context, the suggested matter (*vastu*) characterized by magnanimity—the fact that "you incessantly bestow wealth"—serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning (*vācya*). He explains the phrase "with respect to the threefold suggested" (*tribhedavyaṅgyāpekṣayā*) with the words beginning "triprabheda," and so on.
[The word] *bhaavahala* [is explained as follows].
It is only fitting that not even a moment’s word of consolation was granted to those who had come for refuge, seeking protection as their sole champion while overwhelmed by fear.
The shadow [of the meaning] is as follows: regarding the phrase "this is logical," the use of an interrogative intonation (kāku) implies that "this is not logical.
[This is what is meant by] "cāiaṇa."
Locana bestows newness even when the subject matter has been touched upon by ancient poets;
for instance, there is this ancient verse: "With a body whose strength is exhausted from being passed along the succession of the hands of bards..."
Then, like a miserly woman guarding her treasure, she went along the path of the enemy.

Regarding the novelty [of poetry] arising from the embellishment of the expressed meaning through an ornament or a suggested sense, as in my own verse: "Your hair, resembling a succession of bees intoxicated by spring, served to increase the passion of the sweet-voiced [lover].
How then can it, now radiant with the dust of the cremation ground, bring about even a slight detachment?"

For here, the expressed meaning is embellished by the suggested figures of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) and *vibhāvanā* (poetic anomaly); thus, it possesses novelty despite being connected with an ancient theme.
To illustrate, there is this ancient verse: "Hunger, thirst, desire, envy, and the great fear of death—these five increase even in the wise as they grow old."

Thus, there is novelty through the suggested rasa (sentiment), which, though subordinate, serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning, as in my own verse: "This is not old age; this is surely that serpent of Time, blinded by rage, who hurls forth the foam of manifest poison with his hissing breaths."
Thus he beholds this [world], yet with a heart that considers itself happy; O Śiva, though not seeking worldly gain, alas, alas, such a person is indeed truly steadfast.
Wealth, its body exhausted by the fatigue of passing through the succession of the hands of spendthrifts dear to fools,
sleeps as it were in a state of well-being within the houses of the miserly.
Thus is the shadow [of the verse].
The meaning is clear.
Regarding the word "vasante" (in spring):
This is the speech of someone to a friend:
"The hair is like a succession of bees intoxicated by the spring; that is to say, it is comparable to a continuous series of bees, being exceedingly dark and glossy.
By the phrase 'hair being such as this,' the stage of youth is revealed."
These locks of hair, which were indeed for the increase of your passion,
are like the dust-particles of the cremation ground— resplendent, white, and turned grey by old age.
The various metaphors are employed because they serve as stimulants for both passion (*rāga*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). [The meaning is:
"They do not lead even slightly (*manāk*) to detachment (*viraktaye*), that is, to dispassion.
Thus, the sense is: why is it that dispassion does not arise, even though its causes are present?

On the contrary, by this verse, through the illumination of the meaning that desires increase even in the absence of their causes, and the meaning that the greatness of desire is impossible to describe, the figures of speech *vibhāvanā* (poetic cause) and *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) are suggested; and since these two embellish the expressed meaning (*vācya*), he says: "For here," and so forth.
"Hunger and thirst" (*kṣuttṛṣṇā*) and so forth is a collective dvandva compound. "Old age" (*jarā*) refers to the speech of someone afflicted by the infirmity of aging.
This old age seen upon the head is not [merely] that; this is the serpent of Time, a black snake blinded by fury.
And yet, it is like a serpent in the form of Death;
it scatters—that is, rains down—such froth as clearly contains poison through its hissing.
This is not old age.
But because of the mass of foam showered by the black serpent upon his head,
and because of the reliance on such a case where the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is subordinate to the expressed sound (dhvani),
there is no cessation of the poetic meaning, provided that the quality of creative intuition (pratibhā) is present. (Dhvanyāloka 4.6)
Thus, because of the reliance upon both suggestion (dhvani) and that in which the suggested meaning is subordinate (guṇībhūtavyaṅgya),
there is no cessation of the aesthetic experience of poetry, provided that the quality of creative intuition (pratibhā) is present.

Even though there exist compositions by ancient poets, if one possesses the quality of creative genius (*pratibhā*), then [the work] is successful; but in its absence, there is nothing at all belonging to a poet.
Even the "shadow of composition"—the arrangement of words suited to two meanings—how could it be possible in the absence of the flash of creative genius regarding the meaning?
The claim that this is not "bandhacchāyā" (the mere beauty of composition) because it does not fall into the trap of disregarding the specific meaning is not convincing to those with refined taste.

For if that were the case, then even in the composition of clever and sweet words that disregard the meaning, the *locana* [would have to admit] that the expressed sense (*vācya*) is embellished by a marvelous suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*), and thus becomes beautiful because it serves as a limb for the realization of the sentiment of tranquility (*śāntarasa*). Therefore, novelty remains present even in this ancient verse.
If detachment does not arise in one whose body is worn out by old age, it is certain that death is not firmly established within the heart. // 5 //
This is the commentary (*upaskāra*) on the verse beginning with "satsvapi" and so forth.
Considering the first three quarters to be clear, he recites the fourth quarter—"yadi"—in order to explain it:
for this aforementioned group of manifestations (*pratibhāgaṇa*), being present, becomes more abundant according to the manner described.
But the meaning is not that it is extremely close;
"in that" refers to the quality of intuition having become infinite.
"Not at all.
For everything has already been touched upon by the ancient poets; what, then, remains to be described now, wherein the poet's activity of description might take place?
One might object: "Even if there is nothing unprecedented to be described, nevertheless, the shadow of composition—another term for the arrangement of the maturity of expression—will remain ever-new.
Anticipating the objection that this is why there is such an effort toward other poems in this new house, he says: "The shadow of composition, too..."
The two meanings are the suggested meaning as a subordinate element (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*) and the suggested meaning as the predominant element (*pradhānabhūta*).
"Not more proximate" means that it does not enter the heart more closely.
He states the reason for this: "For if this were so," meaning "O you who are dear to the ignorant. The word *dhruvam* is used in the sense of a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
The word *tat* refers to "people.
Thus, it means those people who have become like foam;
there is also a reading of *phenam iti tad enām iti*.
He perceives [this], yet his heart is otherwise, being happy; and he does not desire the means to liberation (*śivopāya*).
Therefore, the logical connection is: "he is indeed very steadfast. The particle *bata* expresses wonder.
"Jareti" means "therefore" (tad iti), that is, "for that reason.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "Surely there is a firm conviction in the heart that death does not exist. // 5 // // //
Regarding the term *upaskāra* (ornamentation):

the sense is that the phrase "even though [the causes] exist" (*satsvapi*) and so forth connects with the statement "there is no cessation of the aesthetic meaning of the poem" (*na kāvyārthavirāmaḥ*).
He explains the meaning of the passage beginning with "if" (*yadi*) as follows: "being present" (*vidyamāna*), and so on.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the explanation of the term "shadow of composition" (*bandhacchāyā*) is: "the arrangement of words corresponding to two meanings.
The meaning is that the shadow of composition consists of that very form.
The passage beginning with "without regard to... (*anapekṣite*) and so forth is the section containing the objection.
The connection is that "this [definition] is not very close" to those who possess aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).
He raises a further objection with the words "of word and meaning," and so forth.
The locative case in "in the state of being poetry" (*kāvyatve*) is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*).
The meaning is: by reason of word and meaning together constituting poetry.
"Of such a kind" means:
one whose composition of speech is clever and sweet, independent of [external] objects.
Regarding the phrase "the status of poetry" (*kāvyavyavasthā*), the meaning is "the designation as poetry.
He provides the resolution with the words beginning with "others" (*pare*) and so forth.
In the phrase "in its being poetry" (*tatkāvyatve*), the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the opponent.
Regarding the phrase "of poetic compositions," the expression "the conventional usage of its being poetry" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The designation "poetry" would apply. If it is asked: "If poetry consists of the combination of word and meaning, how can there be the status of poetry in such a case [where only one is present]?"—[the answer is: just as the conventional usage of "poetry" applies to the composition of a meaning fashioned by another, so too does it apply to such poetic compositions.

And it is stated in order to demonstrate that the infinity of meaning does not depend solely on the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha), but also on the expressed meaning (vācyārtha): "The infinity of the expressed meaning arises even through the particularities of state, place, time, and so forth;
it is infinite by its very nature, even in its pure form. (Dhvanyāloka 4.7)
Even through distinctions such as state, place, and time,
the denotable object remains infinite by its very nature, even in its pure form.
Even for a pure denoted meaning (*vācya*) that does not require a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*), infinity indeed arises by its very nature.

For this is the inherent nature of denoted objects—whether sentient or insentient—that they become infinite due to differences in state, differences in place, differences in time, and differences in their specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*).

And when these [objects], existing as thus established, are composed even through "Description of Nature" (*svabhāvokti*)—which consists in following well-known multiple natures—the resulting ingenuity of concise composition (*samāsasaṅghaṭanā*) is truly boundless. *Locana*: [The ingenuity of] concise composition.
Sweetness is the absence of harshness.

Regarding the phrase "of such [works]," even if they possess the splendor of unprecedented composition, if they are based on a subject matter composed by another, the conventional designation of "another's poetry" would still apply; therefore, one must take the novelty of the *meaning* (artha) as the basis.
Poetry (*kāvyam*) is that which is worthy of being praised (*kavanīyam*); its state is "poetic nature" (*kāvyatvam*).
However, one should not suspect that this [suffix] is a suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) added to another suffix denoting an abstract state. // 6 // // //
"To establish" means "as a consequence"—this is the ellipsis.

Alternatively, this very point under discussion is stated with the intention that: first, the denoted meaning must be of two kinds to be useful for the suggested meaning; if that [denoted] itself is infinite, then by its very power the infinity of the suggested follows.

Regarding the phrase "of the pure": the sense is that even without contact with the operation whose object is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), [the word] possesses infinity by its very nature alone; subsequently, while remaining infinite in that same nature, it manifests the suggested meaning.

However, one must not think that the suggested meaning is entirely absent there, for if that form which constitutes its very essence were lacking, the designation of "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) would be lost.
Thus, the existence of *rasadhvani* is indeed present in the examples.
He explains the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) as follows: "its own characteristic" (*svālakṣeya*), which means its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
As in the case of form and touch when they exist in an intense state, reside in the same substance, and occur at the same time;
[the word "syāt" (would be)] is the ellipsis for "bālapriyā.
He explains the state [of the eyes] with the verse beginning "apūrvabandha," etc.
He demonstrates the etymological derivation of the term *kāvyatva* (poetic nature) with the words "that which is to be praised" (*kavanīya*), and so forth. // 6 // // //
He explains the word "of the pure" (*śuddhasya*) found in the *kārikā* in order to avoid a misconception— namely, "the manifestation," and so forth. The words "operation" (*vyāpāra*) [are used],
with "of the denoted" (*vācyasya*) understood as the ellipsis.
"Self" (ātman):
the meaning is the non-existence of that which is manifested as a self.
"Loss" (hāni) means non-existence.
Now, one might ask: "What kind of suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arises there? To this, he says: "And thus," and so forth.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "of that which does not depend on a suggested meaning" is also to be explained according to the manner already stated.
[Regarding the phrase] "by them":
"By them," that is, by the expressed meanings;
"right from the very beginning," the poetic meaning is accomplished.

For instance, there is novelty due to the difference in states, as in the *Kumārasambhava*, where the description of the form of the blessed Pārvatī is completed at the very outset with such expressions as "by a collection of all things fit for comparison," yet when she comes within the range of vision of the blessed Śambhu, she is described again through a different turn of phrase as one "wearing ornaments of spring flowers," serving as an implement for the God of Love.

Furthermore, when that very same woman is being adorned at the time of her remarriage, her physical beauty is described in a completely new manner through such expressions as, "Having seated that slender one there facing the east," and so forth;
yet those various modes of description repeatedly employed by that poet for her do not appear redundant, either because they are non-repetitive or because they are filled with ever-new meanings.
This has indeed been demonstrated in the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*: "And their limit does not exist, nor do they appear in any way repetitive."
It is like the delusions of lovers, or the words of clever talkers regarding wealth.

This is another variety of the differentiation of states: that all insentient things possess a second, sentient form, well-known as their "ego" (*abhimānitva*), such as that of Himavat, Gaṅgā, and so forth.
When this [insentient form] is joined with the essential nature of a suitable sentient being and thus described, it becomes something entirely different.
This is just as in the *Kumārasambhava*, in the description of Himavat, whose true nature is that of a mountain.
Furthermore, that which has been demonstrated in the *Saptarṣipriyokti* with respect to the nature of consciousness appears truly unprecedented;
and this is the well-established path of great poets.
This is the *Locana*, and for them, no limit exists.
And yet those delusions of beloveds, or the themes of the speech of great poets, do not appear redundant in any way whatsoever.
The two *ca* particles indicate extreme astonishment.
"In some way" (*katham api*) means that even when investigated with great effort, no tautology is to be found.
Regarding the phrase "of beloveds":

for a fortunate man who has many favorites—much like Rādhāvallabha—even while enjoying various amorous women in a manner made auspicious by his enjoyment, he does not perceive any confusion or redundancy at that time;
this very state is what is called "being beloved."
As for what was said— "in the first creation"— the meaning is that it refers to the first book (*sarga*).
Regarding the word "described" (*upavarṇite*),
the remainder of the sense is "in the third book."
"In the seventh canto" is the ellipsis for "in the *Nirūpitarūpasauṣṭhava*";
the connection is that those modes of description do not shine forth.
"Of that poet" means "of the poet Kālidāsa as well.
He shows the shadow (Sanskrit equivalent) of the passage beginning with "ṇaa" in the *Locana*: "And not," and so forth.
He explains how the amorous gestures (*vibhrama*) of beloved ones are not seen as redundant even in some way with the words "having many favorites" (*bahuvallabha*), and so forth.
The connection is that at that time, he does not perceive the redundancy of the gestures. "At that time" means during the period of enjoyment.
The remainder is that Māghakavi is without cause;
furthermore, the departure [of the poet] for the sake of poetic cultivation has been demonstrated in detail in the *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*.
Moreover, the distinctness of sentient beings through stages such as childhood is well known indeed to good poets.
Even though there is no difference in the general state of volitions (*cetanā*), they are diverse due to differences in their intermediate states,
just as among young women— some whose hearts have been pierced by the flower-arrowed god [of love] and others who are not;
and even among those, some are disciplined and others are undisciplined.

Furthermore, when the individual nature of insentient entities—which are differentiated by various states such as their commencement and so forth—is described one by one, it results in nothing but infinity.

For example: "Those very things which, when swallowed, produced in the cries of swans a certain other kind of resonant, gurgling charm arising from the friction of their rasping throats—those tips of lotus-root joints, now rivaling the tender sprouts of the tusks of young elephants, have emerged in the beds of lotuses."
In this same manner, other cases should also be understood by following this direction.

Regarding the eye: that very form which attains novelty moment after moment is what constitutes its loveliness. And regarding "beloved ones": this particular charm of beautiful women, which flows in a continuous stream throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), appears ever-new and ever-fresh.
For this [love] is not learned from another like the piling of sacrificial fires (agnicayana) and so forth,
by virtue of which it might incur the charge of tautology through similarity to that;
rather, it is merely the blossoming of the sprouts of passion emerging spontaneously— thus, its quality of being ever-new.
