The meaning is that the poetic sense is likewise the natural outflow of one's own innate genius, independent of the instruction of others.
[The author] states the meaning implied by the phrase "the amorous gestures of beloveds" with the words "of the beloveds," and so forth,
and "for not," and so forth.
This is a particular kind of error;
the meaning is that it is not learned in the same way that the piling of the fire-altar (agnicayana) is learned from another source.
"By which" refers to this.
The meaning is "because of having been learned from another.
The word "that" (tat) means "a particular kind of error" (vibhramaviśeṣa).
"Novelty" (navanavatva) refers to that [poetry],
as is understood from the ellipsis "of it.
He explains what was under discussion— "the meanings of the words of good poets"— with the passage beginning "in the same way," and so forth.
"Like that" means it becomes equal to that; the meaning is that it becomes ever-new. In the commentary, this refers to "in relation to the nature of that which is insentient."
The phrase "the description of Himavat" is understood as the subject.
"'That has been shown' means that it has been described."
"In spite of the difference in states" means:
even though there is no difference in the bodily states such as childhood and so forth. "Internal" means: [referring to the internal self].
The meaning is "mental.
Regarding the word "of the swans" (*haṃsānām*),
it means "by those swallowed" (*kabalitaiḥ*), that is, by those eaten.

The construction is as follows: "by which [voices], through the scraping of the throat in the cries of cooing swans, another kind of charm—a gurgling sound—is attached, that is, brought into connection.
And regarding the phrase "even though it exists exactly as it is, it is nevertheless being composed," the word *tāvat* explains the two eyes—beginning with "but at a later time," etc.
First, there is the diversity of form among insentient things due to the difference of location.

Just as it is well known for winds moving through various directions and places, and for other things such as water and flowers, so too among sentient beings— such as humans, cattle, and birds— who are nourished by villages, forests, water, and so forth, a great difference is indeed observed between one another.
And when this difference is analyzed and described according to its specific nature, it remains exactly as it is.

For instance—who could possibly reach the end of the various distinctions among human beings alone, who differ according to direction, place, and so forth, regarding their diverse activities in worldly affairs and the like?
This is especially true for women.
And yet, all of this is depicted by skilled poets exactly as it appears in their creative intuition (*pratibhā*).
Furthermore, there is diversity due to the difference in time;
for example, the insentient directions, the sky, water, and so forth, vary according to the difference in seasons,
and among sentient beings, states such as longing and the like are well known to depend upon specific times.
Furthermore, it is well known that the basis for all things existing within the entire world consists of their specific characteristics (*svālakṣaṇya*) and their various distinctions.
Even when such things are depicted exactly as they exist, they bring about an infinite extent of the poetic subject matter (*kāvyārtha*).
Regarding this, some maintain that objects attain the status of being expressed through their universal nature (*sāmānyātman*), and not through their particular nature (*viśeṣātman*).

For those [poetic descriptions] are composed by poets based solely on the commonality of forms experienced by themselves and others, superimposing the nature of the pleasures and their causes they have personally experienced onto other things;
for they do not perceive—as yogis do—the past, future, or present through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), with all their unique particularities (*svalakṣaṇa*) being unfamiliar and so forth.
And that commonality of the object of experience and the experience itself, being shared by all cognizers, has become the domain of the ancients alone because it is limited.
Because it is impossible for that [suggestion] to be its object.
As for the word "first" (*tāvat*):
later on, indeed, it may attain a supreme variety through contact with the suggested meaning.
The intention of the word "tāvati" (to that extent) is that it is variegated by its very nature;
and "of those causes" refers to the seasons,
garlands, and so forth.
That which is common to both one's own experience and the experiences of others, being devoid of any other particularity, is that "mere" [state]; it is by relying upon that [state]—
and not by those poets—
that this has been said, for the purpose of expressing absolute impossibility.
He explains the phrase "experienced by oneself and others" (*bālapriyā*) with the words beginning "experienced by oneself" (*svānubhūta*).

The meaning of the word *mātra* is clarified as "devoid of other particulars" (*viśeṣāntararahita*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is stated: "the unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as the unfamiliar and so forth."
The meaning is that this refers to the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of objects such as those not previously familiar;
the connection is that "this has been stated.
And the statement beginning with "for not" (*na hi*) and so forth is what is meant by "the explanation."

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of demonstrating absolute impossibility": "absolute" (atyantam) refers to that which is impossible, namely the impossibility of establishing things through their specific individual natures; the meaning is "for that purpose," i.e., for the sake of making that known.
He clarifies this very point with the words beginning with "perception" (pratyakṣa).

Therefore, the mere conceit of those moderns by whom that particular variety is perceived as something new is nothing more than a fabrication; for there is here only a diversity produced by verbal expression. To this it is replied: as for what was said—that the activity of poetry proceeds by relying on mere universals (*sāmānya*), and since these are limited, they have already been made the object of experience long ago, and thus there is no novelty [in the activity of poetry]—that is so.
The claim that "the subject matter of poetry is limited to nine types" is incorrect;
for if poetry proceeds by relying merely upon generalities, then what accounts for the excellence of the poetic themes composed by great poets?

Or rather, there is no designation of "poet" for anyone other than Vālmīki, because there exists no poetic subject matter other than the Universal (sāmānya), and that Universal has already been revealed by the First Poet himself. If it is argued that this is not a fault because of the variety of expression (*ukti-vicitrya*), then what is this "variety of expression"?
For speech (ukti) is a statement that conveys a specific object of expression; when there is variety in that [speech], how could there not be variety in the object of expression?
This is because the two—the expressed and the expresser—function through an inseparable relationship.

Even when there is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), words express that which has been conventionally designated (*saṃketita*); this [convention] is maintained for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
At that time, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist; therefore, for us, there is no convention with respect to that [particular].
By such arguments as these, only the general [meaning] is touched upon.
Why?
The sense is: how can those engaged in the context accept a redundancy of meaning that is not being perceived?
To clarify this very point, he says: "If not...
and "For the statement...
If a specific statement were merely a synonym for that [meaning], then when that meaning is presented in its entirety through other synonyms, one would have no sense of non-redundancy.
"In even the case of direct perception" (*pratyakṣadarśane 'pi*) means:
even when there is direct perception of the true nature of things by poets. "Is touched" (*spṛśyate*)—[is experienced].
The word "kavivāca" (the poet's speech) is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
In the commentary, it says "anubhāvya" (to be experienced):
the meaning is that which is the generality (*sāmānya*), the nature of generality, of both objects to be experienced—that is, those things to be experienced—and of the experiences themselves.
‘Of that’ means: of the generality consisting of the object experienced and the experience itself.
‘In the absence of being an object’—meaning: [in the case where it is not an object].
The word "of the ancients" (purātanānām) is to be supplied [to the relative pronoun].
"Of them" (teṣām) means "of those belonging to the present day."
The connection is that [this] is merely a matter of conceit (*abhimāna-mātra*).

Immediately after the phrase "In this regard, it is said," there follows the reading beginning with "As for what was stated: 'The activity of poetry proceeds by relying on the mere universal (*sāmānya-mātra*)'" and so forth.
However, in some manuscripts, prior to this, there is the passage: "If the activity of poetry proceeds by relying on the mere universal, then in the manner demonstrated therein..."

"The variety of poetry arises from specific circumstances and so forth; why then should it not be considered a mere repetition? If it is not so, how then is there no infinity of poetry?"—this is also a reading [of the text]. To avoid contradicting that, the passage in the *Locana* beginning with "Why then... and ending with "...if it is not so" explains the intent of the section beginning with "For expression is... by means of the words "synonym," etc.
It is merely a different way of expressing the same thing through another word. Therefore,
that [cause] is "unimpaired," meaning without deficiency.
There is no conceit of tautology [in this].
Furthermore, the form of the expressed meanings as they appear in poetry is perceived precisely through the non-differentiation of the specific objects of apprehension.
Therefore, even one who maintains that there is variety in expression, though not wishing to admit variety in the expressed meaning itself, must necessarily accept it.

Thus, this is the summary here: if even for a single person other than Vālmīki, it is admitted that there is creative intuition regarding objects, then that [intuition] would be infinite and inexhaustible.
Furthermore, that which is said to be the basis for the novelty of expression (*ukti-vaicitrya*)—namely, its being unlike ordinary poetry—is entirely consistent with our own position.

For all the various modes previously shown as causes for the infinite diversity of poetic meaning attain a twofold increase precisely through this novelty of expression. And as for this class of ornaments such as simile (*upamā*), paronomasia (*śleṣa*), and so forth, [the sense is that] the distinction lies solely in the expression’s capacity to convey a specific denoted meaning; such is the underlying thought.

Regarding the phrase "the non-difference of the specific object of apprehension" (*grāhyaviśeṣābheda*): the "object of apprehension" (*grāhya*) is that specific feature (*viśeṣa*) which is established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception; its "non-difference" (*abheda*) refers to the identity [of words] with that.

By this, the following meaning is conveyed: the linguistic convention (*samaya*) of words applies to some entity whatsoever—whether it be a universal (*sāmānya*), the locus possessing that universal (*tadvat*), or the exclusion (*apoha*).
What is the use of this further debate?
For who among these disputants would disagree that the specific distinction [of the meaning] is understood from the sentence?

This is because, in all positions regarding the sentence-meaning—whether it be the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*), its opposite, or the distinctions of connection (*saṃsarga*) and so forth—the specific distinction cannot be denied.
And it has been stated that this variety of expression is not merely a matter of synonyms.
Furthermore, he says "moreover" (*kiñca*) to indicate that what follows actually establishes our own position.
The word "again" (*punar*) [is used]...
The meaning is "furthermore. For *nibha*, *pratima*, *chala*, and *pratibimba* are synonyms for *upamā* (simile).
It indeed becomes manifold through various expressions such as "reflection," "equal," "resembling," and "appearing like."
In reality, because there exists a variety of meanings in these utterances,
the word *nibha*— due to its application according to a restrictive rule—
is merely perceived as a tautology; such is the meaning of the phrase "bālapriyā."
"Having a distinguished denotation" (*viśiṣṭavācya*) means "having a specific denotatum" (*vācyaviśeṣa*).
The connection [of the phrase] is with "to be apprehended by means of valid cognitions such as direct perception" (*pratyakṣādipramāṇair grāhya*).
"Therefore, this is the meaning" means that by the aforementioned passage, the meaning about to be explained is established.
[This refers to] the general entity (*sāmānya*) according to the view of the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
In the Nyāya view, convention (*samaya*) pertains to that which possesses the property (*tadvat*); in the Buddhist view, it pertains to the exclusion (*apoha*).
This is according to another system of debate, that is, a specific type of discourse.
The specific nature of that [object] is the specific nature of the thing (*vastu*). Who here could have any disagreement? No one at all.
He states the reason for this with the words beginning "endowed" (*anvita*) and so forth.
The meaning is: "in all those positions, such as anvita-abhidhāna (the theory that words denote meanings already connected), which hold that the sentence-meaning [is primary].
The phrase "because the particularity cannot be denied" implies the word "in perception" (*pratītau*) as a supplement.
The meaning is that the cognition of a specific object cannot be denied.
Regarding the word *punaḥ* in the phrase "due to the variety of repetitions," the explanation is given as *bhūyaḥ*.
The explanation of the intended meaning (*bhāvārtha*) of the passage beginning with "And this which... is provided by the words "simile" (*upamā*) and so forth.
The connection is that "the simile indeed becomes manifold.
Now, one might ask: since words such as *nibha*, *pratima*, and so forth have the same meaning, how can there be such variety? To this he says: "In reality," and so on.
He concludes with: "Thus."
Regarding the word "tat" (that):
the category of *alaṅkāra* (ornaments), being well-known, when composed through the variety of expression (*bhaṇiti*), itself assumes an infinite extent, branching out into hundreds of forms.

Furthermore, since expression is established according to the differences between individual languages, it brings about yet another infinity of poetic meanings by means of the variety of objects within the specific scope of each respective language.
As it has been said by me: "Time passes for people crying out 'Mahamaha!'; therefore, O Janardana, let not the mind become a beggar."

In this way, however one examines them, no limit to the meanings of poetry can be found. However, this is said: the term *pratimā* (image/reflection) is used because it represents that which was previously shown as the "locana" (the eye/sight), serving as a model for the various expressed meanings (*vācya*) distinguished by their states and so forth. Thus, in all cases, the expressed meaning is simply that which is useful for the beginner; due to the inherent flaws in the study of poetic commentaries, there arises the delusion of synonymy among these terms.
This is the intended meaning.
Thus, the infinity of meanings and the infinity of ornaments arise from the variety of expression (*bhaṇiti*).
Furthermore, he will demonstrate that these also arise from other sources by stating "and expression."

The connection is as follows: the object to be expressed (*vācya*) is the domain of a specific language; the diversity produced by that [expression] is the basis and cause for the infinity of poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) and poetic meanings (*kāvyārtha*). Thus, the diversity of expression—which is the object of the action—brings about [the infinity] which is the agent.
Under the guise of qualifying "karma," the cause has been shown:
as one says "mine, mine," time passes; thus the cause has been shown.
Nevertheless, the Lord Janārdana does not become an object of the mind.
"How could the God not come within the range of the mind of one who constantly utters the name 'Madhumathana'?"— this is the shadow of the *virodhālaṅkāra* (figure of contradiction),
brought forth by the expression "mahamaha" in the Saurashtran dialect. // 7 //

The meaning is that there is an infinity of meanings and so forth, which serve as the basis for the various objects of expression distinguished by state (*avasthā*) and other factors. "From that" (*tataḥ*) [refers to this].

The meaning is "due to the variety of expressions. The analysis of the compound *yastā* as a bahuvrīhi is provided by the words "of the ornaments" (*alaṅkārāṇām*) and so forth. [The phrase] "by way of a qualification" (*viśeṣaṇacchalena*) [is explained as follows].
The meaning is: "by way of the qualifiers beginning with 'specifically determined' (*pratiniyata*) and so forth.

He states the shadow [or implied sense] of the passage beginning with "great" (*maha*)—namely, "mine" (*mama*) and so forth—meaning one who says "mine, mine," or says "this is mine," "this belongs to me," and so on.
In this context, "mine" (*mama*) is the literal meaning;
"O slayer of Madhu" (*madhumathana*) is the implied, contradictory meaning;
and "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) indicates the contradiction.
Regarding the phrase "samunmiṣitā": the meaning is that the shadow-form (*chāyā*) of the word *maha-maha* becomes *mama-mama*, and that of *madhu-mathana* becomes *madhumathana*. // 7 // // //

Since the distinction between the *kārikā* and the commentary (*vṛtti*) from this point onward is difficult to discern, he explains both of them separately, beginning with "The state" (*avasthā*), etc.:
"In the object of perception, it is seen as a plenitude; that cannot be excluded."
But that [suggestion] shines forth by virtue of its dependence on rasa.
...that cannot be removed;
rather, it shines forth by virtue of being the substratum for aesthetic flavor (rasa). // 8 //
This is now stated here in brief for the instruction of good poets:

"If the course of events, connected with rasa, bhāva, and so forth, is followed in accordance with propriety (*aucitya*), even when it is differentiated by place, time, and other factors; [then the work succeeds]. (Dhvanyāloka 4.9)
If the course of events, connected with rasa, bhāva, and so forth, is followed in accordance with propriety, it is understood as being distinguished by place, time, and other factors. (9)
What count can there be of other poets whose powers are limited? Even by thousands upon thousands of Vācaspatis, that [work] remains inexhaustible despite diligent effort,
just as the nature of the worlds does not perish.
Even by thousands upon thousands of Vācaspatīs striving with effort, that [nature] cannot be brought to an end, just as the nature of the worlds cannot be destroyed.

For just as the nature of the world, though consisting of a manifold expansion of diverse objects manifested throughout a succession of past kalpas, is seen by the eye only in its totality, yet that [nature] shines forth in the object of perception by virtue of being the locus of aesthetic flavor (rasa).
Thus ends the verse;
the rest of the text is a commentary on the middle portion. // 8 // // //
In this case, however, having restated the meaning of the first three quarters [of the verse], the meaning of the fourth quarter is stated as something new (*apūrva*).
The portion beginning with "tad" and ending with "śaktīnām" serves as an intermediate supplement (*upaskāra*) between the two verses.
He explains the fourth quarter of the second kārikā with the words "yathā hi" (just as). 1, 10.
"But another passage, dear child," means that the passages "what was shown previously" and "that cannot be set aside" are the [intended] texts. // 8 // // //
"Fourth," and so forth;
the meaning is that the sense of the verse "But that appears as the locus of the aesthetic flavor (rasa)" is what is being prescribed here.
"In the two verses" means:
The meaning of the passage beginning with "rasabhāve" and ending with "vācaspati" is that [the work] belongs to two authors.
Regarding the term "upaskāra":
the sense is that if it is composed by other poets, then indeed [it is so].
As for "others," that is, poets other than Vālmīki— what count could there be of them?
The meaning is that they would be beyond counting.
"The fourth foot" means "the foot [which is] like the primordial nature (prakṛti) of the worlds. Thus he explains.
The meaning is that he explains [the point] together with the phrase "it does not reach exhaustion.

The phrase "as it has been said" (yathāhi) refers to the passage beginning with "yathāhi" and ending with "to express" (abhidhātum). The section beginning with "in the same way" (tadvat), however, is an explanation of the meaning of the three quarters of the verse beginning with "Vācaspati."
In the commentary, it says "the material cause of the world" (*jagatprakṛti*); the meaning is that *prakṛti* is that which constitutes the cause of the world.
It says "transcendent" (*atīta*).
The term *aparā* refers to that [intellect] by which there has appeared, throughout the succession of past conceptualizations (*kalpanā*), a manifold expansion (*prapañca*) of diverse objects;
it means that in this [intellect], the power to produce other objects (*aparapadārtha*) has been utterly exhausted (*parikṣīṇa*) or destroyed (*naṣṭa*). // 1, 10 //
Furthermore, it cannot now be asserted that the power to create the objects of others has been utterly exhausted;
for in the very same way, this established tradition of poetry, though enjoyed by infinite poetic minds, does not diminish at present,
but rather increases through ever-new forms of cultivation.
Even though this is the case, there nevertheless frequently occur agreements among those of great intelligence;
for it is established that the cognitions of the wise are indeed consistent with reality.
However,
all of them should be understood by the wise as having manifold forms.
Agreements indeed frequently occur among those of great intelligence, for it is an established fact that the intellects of the wise are concordant;
however, all of them should not be considered as being of a single form by the discerning man. (11)

If it is asked how this is so: "For correspondence is indeed similarity with another; that, moreover, is like a reflection, like the form of a painting, and like [the likeness] of embodied beings to their bodies. (12)
For "correspondence" (saṃvāda) regarding the subject matter of a poem is said to be its similarity with another poetic subject;
that, moreover, is established in three ways: like a reflection of embodied beings, like a painted form, and like a similar body.
For some poetic subject is like a reflection of another embodied entity.
"Locana" refers to the half-verse beginning with "saṃvādāḥ," and "naikarūpatayā" refers to the second [half-verse]. // 11 //
With the thought, "What is this royal command? he raises a doubt: "If it is asked, 'How so?
The answer here is: "For correspondence is similarity with another, and that, moreover, is like a reflection."
It is like the form of a painting, and like [the reflection] of embodied beings in a similar body. // DhvK 4.12 //
For correspondence indeed consists in similarity to another, which is like a reflection, like the form of a painting, and like [the likeness] of embodied beings to one another. (12)
Thus, by this verse;
this [verse] has been explained in the commentary by breaking it down into parts.
It is shown that the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "of embodied beings" (*śarīriṇām*) is to be understood with every sentence.
Regarding the term *śarīriṇaḥ*:
as previously stated in the *Bālapriyā* commentary on the verse beginning with *saṃvādāḥ*,
the first half of the verse consists of the portion from *saṃvādāḥ* up to *sumedhasām*.
The meaning is that this refers to the second half-verse beginning with "naike" and ending with "vipaścite.

Here, one should understand that the phrase "the agreements of the wise" (sumedhasāṃ saṃvādāḥ) intends the sense of "the agreements of the intellects and the poems of the wise"; thus, it should be noted that the commentary states "for this is established" and so forth, as well as "for the agreement of the meaning of the poem is being expressed. //11//
"Having set it aside," [it was] explained in the *Vṛtti*;
the phrase "in some manuscripts" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

For this very reason, it will be stated: "In some manuscripts, the kārikās are seen as unbroken [units]. However, the explanation by breaking them down [into parts] is because 'correspondence (saṃvāda) is indeed similarity with another'; that is, correspondence is said to be the similarity of the meaning of the poem with another poetic subject."
Furthermore, it should be understood that [the self] is like a reflection,
and that [it] is like the reflection of embodied beings, and so forth;
this applies to every statement.
The intended meaning is that the term "of embodied beings" (śarīriṇām) is connected with the three [categories] beginning with the reflection (pratibimba).
Another is like a painting; another is similar to a body.
Among these, the first has a non-different nature, while the one immediately following it has a void nature.
But the third [type of simile], being well-known by its own nature, the wise poet should not discard its lack of similarity with anything else.
In that regard, first is the self that is not other, then immediately after that the self that is void;
but the third is the well-known self. A wise man should not abandon the likeness with others.
In this regard, first of all, the poetic subject matter that is like a reflection must be abandoned by one of sound intellect,
because it lacks a non-different essence and is empty of a real body.
Immediately after that, that which resembles a painting— similar to something else and though endowed with another body— must also be discarded due to its insubstantial nature.
But thirdly, even when there exists a distinct and beautiful body [of the plot], the poet must not abandon the subject matter of the poem, even if it involves a contradiction;

for it cannot be said that an embodied being is truly one and the same as another embodied being, even if they are similar. (The word *pradhānabhūtasya* means "of that which has become the primary element. // 12 //
In that regard, first is the self that is not other; immediately after that is the self that is void;
and third is the well-known self. A wise man should not abandon the latter for the sake of equality with the others.
This is the verse.
That which has a non-different essence—that is, a nature (*svabhāva*) that is not other than the poetry previously composed—shines forth in a form that is precisely untouched by prior poetry;
just as a reflection shines forth in a certain form.
In that form, this is indeed a reflection;
as for what its own nature is, he says here: "devoid of a real body.
For nothing unprecedented has been imagined by him, since even a reflection is exactly like this.
Having thus explained the first type, he explains the second with the words "Immediately after that" (*tadanantaraṃ tu*).
This means the second.
That which has equality with another is described as such.
Regarding the phrase "the empty self":
for when there is an imitation, it is only the cognition of the object being imitated that appears—as in the case of a painting or a statue—and not the cognition of [actual] vermilion and so forth;
furthermore, even that [cognition of the object] does not arise from beauty. This is the intended meaning. //13//
In the *Bālapriyā* commentary, the phrase "of the poetic meaning" (*kāvyārthasya*) has been supplied [from the previous context].
He explains the similarity to something else residing within the poetic meaning with the words beginning "that which by another," etc.
In the three instances beginning with "like a reflection" (*pratibimbavat*), the suffix *-vati* is used after a word ending in the genitive case.

In the case of a reflection, there is a similarity with another [object], namely a similarity with the embodied original (bimba); likewise, in the case of a body that is like a form in a painting, a similarity with the embodied [original] is to be understood.
The phrase "for something indeed" (*kiñcid dhi*) and so forth is a statement explaining the resulting chariot.
In that context, the explanation of the word "of the embodied one" (*śarīriṇaḥ*) is found in the *Locana*: "already previously," and so on.

By the statement, "A poet should not abandon comparison with others," it is implied that the meaning already understood should be explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*); thus it is said, "It should be avoided by one of sound intellect," and "It should be abandoned. // 12 // // //

Lest there be a misunderstanding— that "devoid of a real body" (*tātvika-śarīra-śūnyam*) is merely an explanation of "having no other self" (*ananyātmā*)— the *Locana* explains it with the words beginning "ananya" (not other). The word "appears" (*bhāti*) implies the subject "the poetic theme" (*kāvyavastu*).
He demonstrates its resemblance to a reflection with the words "Just as," and so forth.
By saying "Thus he says," the intention is that the passage beginning with "tāttvika" (real) is not an explanation of the term "ananya-ātman" (of non-different nature).
He states the reason for the emptiness of the body in its ultimate sense with the words "for not," and so forth.
By the word "by him" (tena),
it is meant "by the new poet."
"Unprecedented"— the remainder of the phrase is "the subject matter of poetry.
He establishes its insubstantial nature with the words beginning "for in imitation," and so forth.
"She too" refers to that cognition which is the object of imitation. // 13 //
To establish this very point, it is said:
"Even an object that conforms to its previous state appears all the more intensely when another self exists nearby, like the moon-like face of a slender maiden. (Dhvanyāloka 4.14)
Even though it conforms to its former state, an object appears all the more radiant when another self exists nearby,
like the moonlit face of a slender maiden.
When the Self, which is the essence of reality, exists, even another object that follows its former state appears most vividly;
for an object favored by the ancient and beautiful luster attains supreme beauty like a living body,
and does not appear as a mere tautology.
"The face of the slender maiden is like the luster of the moon.
Thus, the boundaries of sentence-meanings that consist of collections [of words] and possess correspondence have been distinguished.
Now, it is stated in order to demonstrate that there is indeed no fault in poetic subjects that take the form of word-meanings and resemble other entities:

Where an ancient arrangement of subject matter is employed like a composition of syllables and so forth within a new poetic work that flashes forth, it is indeed clearly not faulty. (Dhvanyāloka 4.15)
Where an ancient arrangement of matter is employed like a composition of syllables within a new poetic work that flashes forth, it is indeed clearly not a fault. // 15 //

For even the Lord of Speech cannot fashion any letters or words that are unprecedented; this very [perception] is the eye [of knowledge]. Thus, the third form [of reality] is not to be abandoned. Even when another self exists, an object that conforms to its prior state appears exceedingly slender, like the shadow of the moon upon a face.
Thus, this verse has been read in the commentary (*vṛtti*) as divided [into separate lines].
In some manuscripts, however, the verse is seen to be entirely undivided.
The meaning of the word *ātmanaḥ* has already been determined by the two preceding words, namely *tattvasya* and *sārabhūtasya*. // 14 //
The reading is *sasaṃvādānām*.

However, if the reading is *saṃvādānām*, the connection is made through grammatical non-co-ordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*): "of those [collections] which are the agreements of the collections that take the form of sentence-meanings.
This very point is the explanation of the referent of the word *etat* (this) in the phrase *etad eva* (this alone), namely: "of the third," and so forth. This is the *Bālapriyā* commentary.

The connection is that "the meaning of *ātman* has been determined"; the sense is that the phrase "of the essence of reality" (*tattvasya sārabhūtasya*) is an explanation of the referent of the word *ātman*.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the passage beginning with "in its former state" (*pūrvasthiti*) is itself further explained by the passage beginning with "ancient" (*purāṇa*).
Up to the word "puṣyati" [the compound is explained]. Regarding "purāṇī":
the meaning is that it is favored by a shade that is both ancient and beautiful.
‘Śarīravat’ means equal to the body. // 14 // // //

In the *Locana*, he explains the word "subject matter" (*vastu*) within the phrase "the composition of subject matter" (*vasturacanā*) in the *Kārikā* with the words "by the word 'subject matter' (*vastuśabdena*)," and so forth.
[These subjects] are possible;
indeed, when those very same [subjects] are composed [in this way], they do not contradict the quality of novelty in poetry and the like.
In the same way, the forms of word-meanings consist of *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and other such elements that constitute the true essence of meaning.

Therefore— whatever it may be, even if it is something beautiful, whenever this cognition arises in people that "this is manifesting," a wonder is produced in the hearts of the sensitive (*sahṛdayas*) that "this is some kind of manifestation."
Even when a thing follows the shadow of what preceded it, a skilled poet who composes it in such a manner does not fall into censure. (Dhvanyāloka 4.16)
Even when a subject follows the shadow of what has preceded it, a skilled poet who composes it in such a manner does not fall into censure. (16)
The meanings of words are either the locanam or the caturādayaḥ. As for the phrase "but those": it refers to both syllables (akṣarāṇi) and words (padāni).
"Those very same [letters]" means that they are endowed with that very same form, having not attained even the slightest degree of a different form.
Having thus explained the illustrative portion— "just like the arrangement of letters and so forth"— he applies it to the subject of the illustration with the words "in the same way."
"Consisting of *śleṣa* and so forth" means having the nature of *śleṣa* (punning) and the like.
For words such as *sadvṛtta*, *tejasvin*, *guṇin*, and *dvija* are composed with the shadow of *śleṣa* even by thousands of previous poets.

The preceding passage, ending with "the moon and so forth are fixed as points of comparison; likewise, in the case of those whose form is that of [ordinary] objects, it is impossible to construct anything unprecedented," and so on, should be understood as the intended meaning. // 15 // // //
He explains the word "in the world" as "of sensitive readers.
"Aesthetic wonder" (camatkṛti) means a cognition in which aesthetic relish (āsvāda) is predominant.
He explains the word "abhyujjīhīta" as "it arises"; the meaning is that it emerges.
He shows the very form of the intellect (buddhi) by saying, "this is some kind of manifestation."

Whatever it may be, even that is delightful wherein this cognition arises for people, thinking, "This has manifested as such and such. [The word] "meanings" (arthāḥ) implies "those intended to be expressed" (vivakṣitāḥ). This is the remainder [of the sense].
He explains the passage beginning with "tāni tu" (but those... with the words "akṣarāṇi" (syllables... and so forth.
The explanation of the phrase "tāny evopanibaddhāni" (those very [syllables] are composed) is given by the words "tenaiva" (by that very [means]) and so forth.
The word "vyākhyāya" (having explained) [is thus glossed].
The phrase "na hi" and so forth continues until the end of the passage "virudhyanti"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Regarding "sadvṛtta" and so on:
words such as *sadvṛtta* indeed possess multiple meanings.
"Nibaddhā" and so forth:
the meaning is that the moon and other such things, which were previously employed as objects of comparison (upamāna), are now being employed as objects of comparison by contemporary people.
"Abhisandhānīyam" means [that which is intended].
The meaning is that it is to be supplied.
By the statement "where" (*yatra*) in the verse, the word "there" (*tatra*) is to be supplied and connected with the phrase "in the subject matter of the poem" (*kāvyavastuni*).
Alternatively, there is a reading where "yā tu" (but which) is substituted for "yatra."
In the *kārikā*, the phrase "yadapi" and so forth means:
"yadapi tadapi" refers to whatever object it may be;
"ramyam" means it becomes beautiful in poetry.
He explains the meaning of that term with the words beginning "yatra":
"In which" means in whatever object that has been composed;
the grammatical connection is that this cognition—"this something has manifested"—arises for the world.

Even when an object follows that [original] shadow, a skilled poet, by composing it with a stylistic luster (*bandhacchāyā*) consisting of word-arrangements capable of conveying both the intended suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) and the literal meaning (*vācya*), does not fail to kindle [the aesthetic experience].
Thus, it stands established: let words flow forth, bearing the nectar-like essence of various meanings produced as causes; poets must not succumb to despondency regarding their own faultless domain.
Reflecting that there are ever-new poetic themes and that no merit accrues to a poet in composing upon subjects already fashioned by others,
the blessed Sarasvatī herself arranges for the good poet— whose mind has desisted from the desire to seize the property of others— to construct his work exactly as he wishes. (Dhvanyāloka 4.17)
For one whose mind is free from the desire to take another's property, this blessed Sarasvatī herself arranges the subject matter of the good poet exactly as she wishes. (17)
Even when a thing follows the shadow of what preceded it, a great poet who fashions it accordingly does not incur censure.
Thus the verse has been recited by breaking it into parts. // 16 //
Regarding the phrase "in its own object" (*svaviṣaye*): the meaning is that it does not manifest as being restricted to the present moment.

He recites the second half of the verse, beginning with "the desire to take another's property" (*parasvādānecchā*), together with the preceding commentary—namely, the commentary on the passage starting with "of the world there" (*tatra lokasya*) in the *Vṛtti*. *Bālapriyā*: [This is] the explanation of that [passage].
Regarding the passage beginning with "this throbbing" (*sphuraṇeyam*) and so forth,
he says "the eye of the world" (*locanailokasya*) and so forth to demonstrate this very point.
[The phrase] "having been read by dividing [it]" means...
The meaning is that after the first half of the verse beginning with "yadapi," there follows the reading of the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "sphuraṇeyam";
after that, the reading of the second half of the verse beginning with "anugatamapi";
and immediately following that, the reading of the commentary beginning with "gatam. // 16 //

"Let them be extended. This means they have been measured and weighed; "possessing the nectar-essence of various meanings" means those by which there are various meanings equal to the essence of nectar—the sense being that there are as many [meanings] as there are objects.
As it says in the *Māgha*: "Speech consisting of words as many as are required for the sense. Here, "speech" refers to the forms of poetry;
let them be "extended" by poets—that is, let them be composed in detail.
"In faultless" means free from defects.

"In its own domain," that is, within the subject matter of poetry, poets experience "satisfaction," meaning mental delight; by contrast, "despondency" refers to the state of dejection arising from such thoughts as, "From where indeed shall I bring this unprecedented [idea]? and so forth.
It should not be done; why? To this he says: "In another's property," and so forth.
"Vastu" refers to the poetic composition.
The connection is that [the word] "constructs" refers to a good poet (*sukavi*).

Having clearly understood the meaning of the *kārikā* as "according to the poet's wish" (*yatheṣṭam*), meaning without transgressing what is desired by the poet, [Abhinavagupta] completes the phrase "in his own domain" (*svaviṣaye*) in the *Locana*, stating: "not manifesting itself at that moment" (*svayaṃ tātkālikatvenāsphuritaḥ*).
The meaning is: not manifesting to the poet at that time.
By this, the reason for the member [of the syllogism] is shown:
"he recites together with the preceding preparation.

Immediately after the recitation of the first half of the verse, there exist those whose minds are restrained from the desire to take what belongs to others; for such a good poet, this blessed Sarasvatī joins the subject matter exactly as desired.

For those great poets whose activity proceeds by virtue of the ripening of past merit and long-standing practice, their own labor is of no use whatsoever, as they are free from desire for appropriating meanings composed by others;
that very goddess Sarasvatī herself manifests the intended meaning.
For this indeed is the nature of the great poetry of the great poets—thus it is concluded.

"Because, from that which possesses the beauty of qualities and ornaments appropriate to its basis of unafflicted aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), every desired object is attained by the virtuous"—this is the third quarter [of the verse], "the subject matter of a good poet. For what reason might one not be diligent, thinking, "Whence indeed shall I bring something unprecedented?", or become a borrower of subject matter composed by others? Anticipating this extreme concern, he says: "Sarasvatī herself... [is the source].
With the intention that the word *suveḥ* in the *kārikā* is a singular used in the sense of a genus (*jātāvekavacana*), he explains it as "of good poets" (*sukavinām*).
He clarifies this very point with the passage beginning "by former...
and ending with "not of them."
"Manifests" means that it creates something entirely new. // 17 // // //
"Thus" (iti) means by way of the method of defining the verse and its commentary.
Poetry bears that splendor which arises from those qualities and ornaments that are appropriate and unafflicted when based upon aesthetic flavor (rasa).

It bears that splendor which arises from the garden— a garden that is untiring, timely, and radiant through the performance of watering and other such tasks— and from the ornamentation of its qualities, such as tenderness, luster, and fragrance, which is produced by and dependent upon that [garden] and serves as the cause for their perfection. "From which" refers to the garden known as Kāvya.

"All desired" means characterized by proficiency, fame, and joy; this is the reading of the commentary (*vṛtti*) from the beginning up to the end of the phrase "having cultivated [the mind] through such states."
The sense is that the word "ceased" (*virata*) is connected to the phrase "whose mind has ceased the desire to take what belongs to others.
He introduces [the next section] with "Why? and so forth; "by intention" means by thought.
"Devoid of effort" means lacking exertion regarding the subject matter of poetry.
"It would be"— why would it not be so?
The meaning is "it would indeed be so. // 17 //
This is an explanation of the word "iti" found in the verse beginning with "ity akliṣṭa": "kārikā" and so forth.
The meaning is: "in the manner of that exposition which consists of both the *kārikā* and its commentary (*vṛtti*).
This connects with the phrase "the resonance (*dhvani*) of this has been shown."

Showing that "unwearied" (*akliṣṭā*) is an epithet of *śobhā* (beauty) and that "appropriate to the locus of the aesthetic flavor" (*rasāśrayocitā*) is an epithet of both *guṇas* (qualities) and *alaṃkāras* (ornaments), he explains [the verse] with the words beginning "unwearied. "From that" means "having the qualities and ornaments as its cause."
"Produced by that" means "impelled by that.

For it is through watering appropriate to the season that a garden— consisting of a collection of creepers, trees, and so forth— attains the perfection of qualities such as tenderness, by means of the abundance of shoots, leaves, flowers, and the like.
With the intention that the word *alaṃ* here denotes sufficiency (*paryāptatā*), he explains it as "the act of making sufficient.
This means the attainment of fullness.

May this very resonance (*dhvani*), which has been revealed in the poetic commentary—the abode of all bliss and a celestial garden—possessing a greatness equal in measure to a *kalpa*, be enjoyed by those of noble soul.

When this [work] existed as if long dormant within the minds of those of mature intellect—following the path of the principles of the essence of true poetry—all of this has already been explained at length; thus, only the meaning of the verse is here commented upon. Regarding the phrase "by those of virtuous deeds":

The meaning is: by those who, even without instruction involving hardship, are recipients of such fruits. "In the abode of all happiness" means: in the sole sanctuary of that happiness which is entirely unadulterated by even a trace of suffering.
The sense is that that which is both entirely pleasing and entirely beneficial is difficult to find in this world.
The "garden of the wise" is Nandana;
it is the cause for the attainment of desired objects only for those who have performed meritorious deeds such as the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
And the wise ones, who know the principles of poetry,
have shown that [the meaning] was already present and merely manifested.
"Shown" means it was revealed while remaining exactly as it was.
For how can that which is not manifested possess the quality of being an object of enjoyment?
[The compound] "one whose greatness is such as to be comparable to the wish-fulfilling tree" (kalpatarūpamāna-yasya-tādṛṅ-mahimā-yasya) is a *bahuvrīhi* containing within it another *bahuvrīhi*.
Indeed, the attainment of all desired objects in poetry is entirely dependent upon that [greatness].
And this has been explained in detail.
When the path of the principles of true poetry had long been abandoned from the minds of those with mature intellects,

[the author] says "those who partake in such fruits" (*bālapriyā*); that is to say, they partake in fruits such as proficiency (*vyutpatti*) and the like— meaning those whose nature is to partake in them, or who are worthy of them.
"By them" means by the princes and so forth; here,
the word *khila* has the meaning of "suffering."

With the intention that it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that in which there is no stubbornness (*khila*), thus it is 'free from stubbornness' (*akhila*)," he explains with the words beginning "suffering" (*duḥkha*) and so forth.
He states the [positive] state (*bhāva*) with the words beginning "all objects" (*sarvārtha*) and so forth.

By the phrase beginning "one who has performed the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice" (*kṛtajyotiṣṭoma*), the meaning of the term "virtuous person" (*sukṛtin*) is explained according to the interpretation of the garden (*udyāna*).
With the intention that, just as in the case of a garden, the connection with the meaning of the word *vibudha* is intended here by implication for poetry as well, he says "vibudhāśca" and so forth.
The construction is "those who know the essence of poetry. By the word "ca" (and), the sense of "gods" is conjoined.
Showing that [the word] "shown" (*darśita*) serves to establish its being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*), he says: "of that which is unmanifest," and so forth.
With the intention that the word "comparison" (*upamāna*) signifies the act of comparing (*upamiti*), he provides the analysis: "the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*)," and so forth.
However, if the word "comparison" signifies the instrument of comparison (*upamitikaraṇa*), the analysis is: "the wish-fulfilling tree is the comparison."
Regarding the term *bahuvrīhi*:

although here the word "greatness" (*mahiman*) conveys the similarity to the Kalpataru tree, it should be understood that its ultimate application lies in the *dhvani* (suggested meaning), which is the locus of that greatness.
The sense is that poetry is equal to the Nandana grove, and *dhvani* is equal to the Kalpataru tree.
Therefore, demonstrating the grounds for the comparison of *dhvani* to a wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*), he says "all," and so forth.
"Desired" refers to pleasure and the like.
"Dependent on that alone" means being produced solely by *dhvani*.
"In good poetry" (satkāvye): this means the path of logic, the proper course, the collection of arguments that establishes the nature of *dhvani* as being good poetry.
"Cire" means that, starting from a long time ago, it has been as if dormant, clearly unmanifest;
"of those with mature intellects" refers to the former authors of treatises who have reached the culmination of supreme knowledge.
The word "that" refers to the nature of sound; he, whose renowned name is Ānandavardhana, brought that forth for the sake of attaining the awakening of those with sensitive hearts.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Dhvanyāloka composed by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Ānandavardhana; this work is now complete.

"He elucidated that *Locana* for the sake of attaining the awakening of the heart"—this is the conclusion regarding the connection (*sambandha*), the subject matter (*abhidheya*), and the purpose (*prayojana*).
In this world, people for the most part act on the strength of a conviction based on worldly renown;
and that conviction arises through the hearing of a name, accompanied by the recollection of his well-known conduct, poetic skill, scholarship, and so forth.

For instance, this was composed by Bhartṛhari: "He whose greatness of magnanimity is such that in this very treatise such an essence is seen—this composition of verses belongs to him; therefore, this [work] is to be respected. Thus, the world is seen to proceed [according to this].
And the world must necessarily be made to proceed for the sake of attaining the purpose declared in that treatise.
Since it serves as a means to engage the audience who are to be favored by the work, authors record their own names; with this intention, he says "Ānandavardhana.
By the word "renowned" (prathita), it is meant that this very work—which is beneficial for children and possesses a collection of sound arguments—is renowned.
‘Vyākarot’ means he elucidated. Regarding ‘sahṛdaya’:

it is for the sake of attaining that joy which is the ‘udaya’—the spiritual elevation—of those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdayas), namely, the delight caused by the awakening to the true nature of *dhvani*.
The meaning is "for the purpose of attaining that gain which is its nature.
This conclusion is consistent with the opening statement, "Therefore, we describe its true nature for the delight of the hearts of connoisseurs.
Considering the meaning of the verse to be clear, [the author] explains the portion that remains to be stated in the *Locana* with the words beginning "satkāvya... (in good poetry, etc.).
This is the conclusion regarding the relationship, the subject matter, and the purpose.
The relationship is that between this treatise and the nature of *dhvani*, characterized as that of the expounder and the expounded.
The subject matter is the nature of *dhvani*.
The purpose is the joy caused by the knowledge of the true nature of *dhvani*.
Since this has been clearly stated by the phrase "for the sake of attaining the delight arising in the hearts of connoisseurs," the subject matter and the purpose are explicitly expressed;
the relationship [between them], however, is understood by implication.
Now he introduces the fourth quarter, beginning with "Then, Ānanda," and so forth, with the words "here" and so on.
Regarding the term "a conviction of possibility":
it means a sense of great esteem.
"By name" means by virtue of the mention of the author's name. "Renowned" [means as follows].
"Another" means something different from the name; or rather, it means "well-known" or "uncommon.
Such is his conduct—that is, the conduct of the author related to him—namely, good conduct (*sadācāra*); the meaning is "by means of recollecting that [conduct]."
And that becomes a cognition of probability; thus is the connection [of the sentence].
He states [the point] with an illustration, beginning with "For instance" (*tathāhi*);
the passage beginning with "This was done by Bhartṛhari" is a description of the form of worldly cognition.
"Of whom" refers to Bhartṛhari;
"this" is a statement directed toward the work [of that name];
and "thus" [indicates the manner of the citation].
The meaning is "by means of such an understanding.
The grammatical connection is that one should proceed toward [the goal] for the sake of accomplishment (*sampatti*).
That very hearing of the name brings about the cessation [of suffering] for some; this is the *Locana*.
One should not take that manifestation of stinginess into account here;

for even if some person, blinded by passion, were to turn away from the sacred scripture (śruta) solely because it has liberation as its purpose, would that make the purpose any less of a purpose? Indeed, the purpose must necessarily be stated.
Therefore, it is well known that [stating the purpose] is a factor for the engagement of those who seek [the truth].
It bestows an outward expansion that makes manifest the manifold variety of meanings.
I salute the fourth power, which reveals the directly perceived reality.

May that eye of Abhinavagupta be employed, which— by fashioning the true essence of the light of poetry through the expansion of Ānandavardhana’s discernment— reveals all existing objects as they unfold, and whose core is that which is to be inferred.
"Bālapriyā" explains "taditi" as meaning "therefore.
"Etadeva prathitam" means "this very thing is well-known."
The meaning is that what has already been stated is now being elucidated;
that very thing is the hearing of the name. It is precisely this hearing of the name that instigates the activity of many.
The meaning is that it is precisely the hearing of that name;
"it effects" means it produces;
"for the sake of the supreme good" (niḥśreyasa).
The meaning is: "from that which has *niḥśreyasa* (the supreme good) as its purpose.
Regarding the word *śrutāt*: the meaning is "from knowledge [of] reality (*tattva*) as presented by the sacred scriptures (*śruti*)."
"By this much" means by the mere cessation of the blindness of passion (*rāgāndha*).
"The purpose" means...
In reality, this means "the purpose. "Aimless" (aprayojana) means distinct from a purpose.
The connection [of the sentence] is: "What indeed would have to be stated?"
The sense is that it should not be stated [otherwise].
The connection is that what is "well-known" (*prathita*) is a factor for the application of a name.
At the end of the first chapter, the author offered salutation to Parā; at the end of the second chapter, to Paśyantī; and at the end of the third chapter, to Madhyamā.
At the end of the fourth chapter, he performs a salutation to Vaikharī, beginning with the words "sphuṭī" and so forth. [The meaning is:

she who bestows that outward diffusion—the manifestation among listeners—of those various meanings (*vicitrārtha*) which are the diversities of sense (*arthavaicitrya*) made manifest by the mouth and clarified within the mind.
[She is called] "Pratyakṣā" (the perceptible).
"Directly perceived" (*pratyakṣam*) means as if showing the object;
that is to say, it shows even objects that are not directly perceived as if they were directly perceived.
"The fourth power" (*turyīṃ śaktim*) refers to the power in the form of *vaikharī*.
"I salute" is the meaning. "Ānandeta":

because of the composition—that is, the joining together—of those essential truths (arthatattva), which are the core meanings of the world of poetry that is expanding and manifesting through the *viveka* (discriminative discernment) of Ānandavardhana, which consists in the comprehension of each respective object as it is distinguished.

That which possesses the excellence that is the very essence of the inferable, and moreover, which, while manifesting and shining forth among those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), shines forth intensely, [reveals] all the true subjects— the essential meanings—
of all poetic works and the like; or alternatively, all the true subjects of all [works].
It is "of that kind" because it illuminates all the virtuous subjects and essential meanings of all poetic works and the like— or rather, all existing entities that constitute virtuous subjects—
belonging to Abhinavagupta, who bears that name.

And yet, a fresh, new, secret—that is, unknown to others—eye, meaning insight or knowledge, was employed; that is, it was put to use by herself. This is the *laṅ* (imperfect) in the passive voice from the causative (*ṇijanta*) form.
Here, a similarity between knowledge and the eye is implied.

"Śrīsiddhi," etc.: He who was purified by the pollen of the lotus-feet of the venerable teacher named Śrīsiddhicela; he whose intellect was refined by a small portion of the mind of Bhaṭṭendurāja, who was purified by the pollen of the lotus-feet of Śrīsiddhicela; he who is a master of speech, logic, and words; and who delights in the service of great compositions—he has composed this "Vastuvṛtti" on the Path.
Does this poet beg the virtuous for the sake of delighting them, as if he were a hare begging the moon?
Nor does he repeatedly censure the wicked; for fire, even when reviled, does not become cold.
In reality, within the heart that consists of Śiva, everything shines forth everywhere as consisting of Śiva;
there is no word of anyone anywhere that is not Śiva. Therefore, may your state become one consisting of Śiva.
Thus ends the fourth Uddyota in the *Kāvyālokalocana* composed by the great Mahāmaheśvara Abhinavagupta; and here this work is concluded.
*Bālapriyā*: Bhaṭṭendurāja; he is one whose slight portion of awakening (*buddhileśa*) has been refined by the thought and knowledge of that [teacher].
Regarding the word *vākya*:
the "sentence" (*vākya*) refers to the Mīmāṃsā treatise.
The meaning is that he is the guru of those who know the *pramāṇa*, which is the treatise on logic (*nyāyaśāstra*), and the *pada*, which is the treatise on grammar (*vyākaraṇaśāstra*).
He for whom there is a relish (*rasa*) in the service of this treatise—
[Abhinavagupta], it is implied— is the one [who composed] the *Dhvanivastuvṛtti*, a commentary on the work *Dhvani*.
"vyaracayat" means he composed. "Sajjanān" (the virtuous) is a statement made by this poet, referring to himself.
He does not beg from the virtuous for his own pleasure, as he already possesses the very respect for his own work that brings him joy;
to dispel the doubt as to why he does not beg, he provides an illustration: "Why was the moon requested?
The word "for the sake of delight" (*hlādanāya*) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].
"Requested by whom? means "requested by people"; the sense is "not at all.
The meaning is that, like the moon, a virtuous person gladdens others of their own accord; thus, gladdening others is the very nature of a virtuous person, just as it is of the moon.
"Not at all.
Even though he has been repeatedly censured by the wicked— indeed, even though he has been repeatedly reviled—
the word "this poet" is to be supplied [as the subject].
He asks why he does not criticize the wicked at all, and for this reason says "not indeed," and so forth.
*Anala* means fire; *śītala* means not hot (*anuṣṇa*).
For just as fire is always of a hot nature, so too is a base person always of a nature to find fault in others; and the meaning is that this nature is unavoidable.
The word "therefore" (ataḥ) is connected with the preceding clause in both cases.

Now, the author of the work, who is a supreme devotee of Maheśvara, at the conclusion of the book, while performing the supreme auspicious rite consisting of the contemplation of Paramaśiva, says "In reality," and so forth:
when the heart (*hṛdaya*) of a person is in reality composed of Śiva— or alternatively, when the heart is composed of Śiva—
then every object everywhere shines forth clearly as being composed of Śiva.
"Nothing inauspicious," and so forth:
the meaning is that nowhere at all does the speech of anyone become inauspicious; rather, it is auspicious everywhere.

By this, it is shown that in reality, within his own heart which consists of Śiva, everything shines as consisting of Śiva; therefore, the meaning demonstrated is that even regarding every object, his own speech is indeed auspicious (śiva).
"By that" [refers to this].
The meaning is "by one's own words.
The word *va* is an address directed toward the listeners.
"May there be a state consisting of Śiva, consisting of auspiciousness"—may all be *śiva*. All is auspicious.
May the Goddess of Speech be victorious together with the wise and excellent poets;
and may the *Kāvyāloka*, along with the Eye [of the Lord], be dear to those of refined intellect.
He was the first among the ocean-like kings of all sciences and great royal sages to receive the honorific title beginning with "Hṛdayatilaka" and others.
Naya was honored by the son of the illustrious emperor Aṅgala;
he was the commentator on the *Śākuntalā* and other works, and he was the preceptor of Gośrīśa and others.
The crest-jewel of those learned in the scriptures and literature, named Parīkṣitopana, a virtuous friend and fellow-student, Gośrīśa, is his support in every respect.
I, Śāraka, known by the name Rāma, have composed this commentary;
may it be dear to young students in the year [measured by] arrows, fires, sky, and eyes (1535).
Where is the mature eye, and where am I, of dull intellect? Thus, there may be many errors here in the commentary; therefore, let this be corrected by the wise.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Bālapriyā*, a commentary on the *Kāvyālokāloka-ṭippaṇī*, composed by Śāraka, named Rāma, who bears the two titles of *Paṇḍitarāja* and *Sahṛdayatilaka*.
This work is hereby completed.
